JDK, JRE and JVM — Roles and Differences
sections.content:
# JDK, JRE and JVM — Roles and Differences

The JVM, JRE and JDK are related parts of the Java platform, but they have different responsibilities.

The Java Virtual Machine executes Java bytecode. It loads classes, verifies bytecode, manages runtime memory, executes threads and performs garbage collection. JVM implementations are specific to operating systems and processor architectures, even though Java bytecode is designed to be portable.

The Java Runtime Environment traditionally describes the JVM together with the libraries and supporting files required to run Java applications. A machine that only executes an already-built application needs runtime capabilities, not necessarily compiler tools. Modern Java distributions do not always provide a separate JRE download; teams often use a JDK distribution or create a reduced runtime image.

The Java Development Kit includes runtime capabilities and development tools. Important tools include `javac` for compilation, `java` for launching programs, `jar` for archive operations, and diagnostic tools such as `jcmd` and `jstack`.

Check the installed tools:

```bash
java -version
javac -version
```

`java -version` reports the runtime launcher version. `javac -version` reports the compiler version. If the first command works but the second does not, the machine may lack compiler tools or its JDK `bin` directory may not be configured in PATH.

Typical responsibilities:

- JVM: executes bytecode and manages runtime behavior.
- JRE: provides the environment required to run Java applications.
- JDK: provides development, compilation and diagnostic tools alongside runtime capabilities.

A CI build agent normally needs a JDK because it compiles and tests source code. A runtime container may use a smaller runtime-focused image if compilation has already completed. Keep the build and runtime versions compatible, verify the actual image contents and use controlled image versions rather than depending on an unpinned `latest` tag.

sections.title: Java Source Code, Compilation and Bytecode
sections.content:
# Java Source Code, Compilation and Bytecode

Java source code is normally stored in `.java` files. The Java compiler translates valid source code into bytecode stored in `.class` files. Bytecode is an instruction format understood by a compatible JVM rather than native instructions for one particular operating system.

Create `Greeting.java`:

```java
public class Greeting {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String message = "Build completed";
        System.out.println(message);
    }
}
```

Compile the source:

```bash
javac Greeting.java
```

A successful compilation creates `Greeting.class`. Launch it with:

```bash
java Greeting
```

The launcher locates the class, starts the JVM and invokes its `main` method. Supply the class name without the `.class` extension.

Compilation checks syntax, type compatibility, access rules and other language constraints. A compilation error prevents the affected class from being generated. Successful compilation does not guarantee correct business behavior: runtime exceptions, incorrect logic, missing configuration and unavailable external services can still cause failures.

Compiled output can be placed in a separate directory:

```bash
javac -d out Greeting.java
java -cp out Greeting
```

The `-d` option selects the output directory. The `-cp` option specifies the classpath used to locate classes and dependencies.

Java applications are often packaged into JAR archives. A JAR can contain compiled classes, resources and metadata describing the entry point. Build tools such as Maven and Gradle automate compilation, dependency resolution, testing and packaging.

In CI/CD, compile and test using a known JDK, package the tested output and publish the resulting artifact. Promote the same artifact through environments instead of rebuilding different binaries for development, staging and production. This makes releases easier to reproduce and investigate.

sections.content:
# Packages, Imports and Access Modifiers

Packages organize related Java types into namespaces. They help prevent naming conflicts and provide a structure for large applications. A package declaration normally appears at the beginning of a Java source file.

```java
package com.example.payment;

public class PaymentService {
}
```

The package name usually corresponds to a directory structure under the source root:

```text
src/
  main/
    java/
      com/
        example/
          payment/
            PaymentService.java
```

The `import` statement allows a type to be referred to by its simple name instead of its fully qualified name.

```java
import java.util.List;
import java.util.ArrayList;

List<String> services = new ArrayList<>();
```

Java provides access modifiers that control where classes and members can be accessed. `public` allows access wherever the declaring type is accessible. `private` restricts access to the declaring class. `protected` allows access within the package and through subclass access rules. A member with no explicit modifier has package-private access.

Top-level classes can be public or package-private. Only one public top-level class is normally declared in a source file, and the filename must match that public class name.

Use packages to reflect application responsibilities, such as controllers, services, repositories, domain models and configuration. Avoid placing every class in one package or creating excessively deep package structures without a clear reason.

Access modifiers support encapsulation. Keep implementation details private and expose only the operations that other parts of the application genuinely need. This reduces accidental coupling and makes refactoring safer.

sections.content:
# Java Development and Execution Workflow

A Java development workflow moves source code through editing, compilation, testing, packaging and execution. A developer typically writes source files under a source directory, declares dependencies, compiles the code and runs automated tests before packaging an application.

A simple command-line workflow is:

```bash
javac -d out src/HelloJava.java
java -cp out HelloJava
```

Real applications usually have multiple classes and external libraries. Build tools such as Maven and Gradle provide dependency management, standard directory layouts, build lifecycles, test execution and artifact packaging.

A typical Maven workflow includes:

```bash
mvn clean
mvn test
mvn package
```

`clean` removes generated build output. `test` compiles and executes tests. `package` creates the configured distributable artifact after the required earlier lifecycle phases.

A CI pipeline should use a controlled JDK version, restore dependencies from approved repositories, compile the source, execute automated tests, inspect test results and publish the packaged artifact. Build failures should stop promotion rather than silently allowing an unverified artifact to reach production.

The runtime environment then launches the packaged application using a compatible Java runtime. Configuration such as ports, database addresses and credentials should be supplied through controlled environment-specific configuration rather than hardcoded into source code.

Keep build logs, test reports, artifact checksums and version information. These records help identify which source revision and build produced a deployed application. Reproducible build inputs and immutable artifacts make release investigation and rollback more reliable.

sections.title: Java Language Troubleshooting and Best Practices
sections.content:
# Java Language Troubleshooting and Best Practices

Java failures can occur during compilation, application startup or runtime execution. Identify the failure stage before changing code or configuration.

Compilation errors often include invalid syntax, missing imports, incompatible types, inaccessible members or unsupported language features. Check the compiler output and confirm that the configured JDK supports the source version used by the project.

Runtime exceptions occur after the application starts executing. Common examples include `NullPointerException`, `NumberFormatException`, `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` and `ClassCastException`. Read the exception type, message and stack trace. The first application-owned stack frame often points toward the code that needs investigation.

A missing class at runtime may produce `ClassNotFoundException` or `NoClassDefFoundError`. Check whether the required dependency is included in the packaged artifact and available through the runtime classpath or module path.

Useful checks include:

```bash
java -version
javac -version
jar --list --file application.jar
```

For a packaged application, inspect the archive contents and verify that the required classes and resources are present. Compare the Java version, startup command, environment variables and dependency versions between a working environment and the failing environment.

Follow these practices:

- Use meaningful class, method and variable names.
- Keep methods focused and avoid unnecessary complexity.
- Validate external input and configuration.
- Prefer explicit types and clear control flow.
- Use `equals()` for object content comparison.
- Handle exceptions at appropriate application boundaries.
- Avoid swallowing exceptions without logging or recovery.
- Write tests for normal behavior, invalid input and boundary conditions.
- Keep Java versions and dependencies controlled in CI/CD.
- Never hardcode production credentials in source code.

A useful troubleshooting process reproduces the problem, captures the exact error, identifies the failing layer, verifies assumptions and tests the correction. Avoid changing multiple unrelated settings at once because that makes the actual cause harder to identify.

sections.title: Java Project Layout and Directory Conventions
sections.content:
# Java Project Layout and Directory Conventions

A Java project layout defines where source code, tests, configuration files, documentation and generated artifacts are stored. A consistent layout makes a project easier to understand, build, test, review and maintain. It also allows build tools and IDEs to discover files using predictable conventions.

A typical Maven-style Java project uses this structure:

```text
payment-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/
│   │   │   └── com/example/payment/
│   │   │       └── PaymentApplication.java
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       ├── java/
│       │   └── com/example/payment/
│       └── resources/
├── target/
└── README.md
```

The `src/main/java` directory contains application source code. `src/main/resources` contains files needed by the application, such as properties, YAML configuration, templates and static resources. `src/test/java` contains automated test source code. `src/test/resources` contains test-specific input files and configuration. The `target` directory is generated by Maven and normally should not be committed to source control.

The root directory contains project-level files such as `pom.xml`, `.gitignore`, README documentation and build configuration. A project may also contain deployment manifests, Dockerfiles and CI pipeline definitions.

The standard layout is a convention, not a requirement of the Java language. Build tools can be configured to use alternative directories, but following established conventions reduces custom configuration and makes onboarding easier.

For DevOps teams, predictable project layout helps CI systems locate source files, execute tests, package resources and publish artifacts consistently.

sections.title: Source Roots and Resource Directories
sections.content:
# Source Roots and Resource Directories

A source root is a directory that a build tool treats as the starting point for discovering source files. In a standard Maven project, `src/main/java` is the main Java source root and `src/test/java` is the test source root.

Java files under a source root are compiled into class files. Their package declarations determine their logical namespace and normally correspond to subdirectories below the source root.

For example:

```text
src/main/java/
└── com/
    └── example/
        └── payment/
            └── PaymentService.java
```

The source file should declare:

```java
package com.example.payment;
```

Resources are different from Java source files. Files under `src/main/resources` are copied into the application's output so they can be loaded at runtime. Examples include `application.properties`, `application.yml`, logging configuration, message bundles and static templates.

Test resources belong under `src/test/resources`. They may contain sample JSON, SQL initialization scripts, certificates for controlled tests or test configuration. They should not accidentally be included as production application resources.

Maven's standard resource and source directory conventions allow a project to build without manually specifying every directory. If a project uses non-standard paths, configure them explicitly in the build file and verify that the intended files are included.

A common mistake is placing configuration files in the repository root and assuming they will automatically be available inside the packaged JAR. They are not necessarily copied as application resources. Put runtime classpath resources in the appropriate resources directory or explicitly configure how they are packaged.

Inspect the generated output after building. Confirm that required configuration files and compiled classes exist in the expected locations. This catches missing-resource problems before deployment.

sections.title: Package Naming and Namespace Organization
sections.content:
# Package Naming and Namespace Organization

Java packages organize classes and interfaces into namespaces. They prevent unrelated classes from having to share one global class name and provide a logical structure for application code.

A package declaration appears at the beginning of a Java source file:

```java
package com.example.payment.service;

public class PaymentService {
}
```

The corresponding directory structure normally looks like:

```text
src/main/java/com/example/payment/service/PaymentService.java
```

Package names are conventionally written in lowercase. Organizations commonly use a reversed domain name, such as `com.example`, as the beginning of their package namespace. This reduces the possibility of collisions with classes from other organizations.

A layered application might use packages such as:

```text
com.example.payment
├── controller
├── service
├── repository
├── domain
├── dto
└── config
```

The controller package handles incoming requests, the service package contains application operations, the repository package handles persistence access, and the domain package represents core business concepts. DTO packages contain request or response data structures, while config contains application configuration classes.

Package organization should reflect actual responsibilities. Do not create dozens of empty packages just to make the directory tree look complex. Also avoid placing unrelated classes into one large package.

Packages are not a replacement for access control or architecture enforcement. Classes in the same package can access package-private members, so package boundaries should be designed deliberately.

In large applications, clear package organization helps developers identify where a change belongs, reduces accidental dependencies and supports code review. Build and test teams can also use package conventions when configuring test discovery and static analysis.

Test Source and Test Resource Organization
sections.content:
# Test Source and Test Resource Organization

Java projects separate production code from automated test code so that test-only classes and dependencies do not become part of the production application unintentionally.

In a Maven project, production source code belongs under `src/main/java`, while test source code belongs under `src/test/java`. Test input files and test configuration belong under `src/test/resources`.

Example:

```text
src/
├── main/
│   ├── java/com/example/payment/
│   │   └── PaymentService.java
│   └── resources/
│       └── application.yml
└── test/
    ├── java/com/example/payment/
    │   └── PaymentServiceTest.java
    └── resources/
        └── payment-test-data.json
```

A unit test might verify a calculation without starting a database or web server:

```java
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;

class PaymentServiceTest {
    @Test
    void calculatesTotal() {
        PaymentService service = new PaymentService();
        assertEquals(200, service.calculateTotal(100, 2));
    }
}
```

The test framework discovers and executes the test based on its configuration and naming conventions. Maven's test lifecycle uses the configured test provider and plugins to compile and run these tests.

Keep test data in test resources rather than hardcoding large fixtures throughout test methods. Use separate test configuration for database URLs, mock endpoints and other test-only settings. Never put production secrets into test resources or commit real credentials.

A CI pipeline should compile test sources and execute the test suite before packaging or publishing the application. Review test reports and ensure that a failing test causes the pipeline to fail. Clear separation between production and test directories makes the build more predictable and prevents test-only files from leaking into production artifacts.

sections.title: Build Files and Project Metadata
sections.content:
# Build Files and Project Metadata

A Java build file describes how a project is compiled, tested, packaged and connected to external libraries. Maven uses a Project Object Model file named `pom.xml`. Gradle commonly uses `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts`.

A minimal Maven project definition looks like:

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
         https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>payment-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>
</project>
```

The `groupId` identifies the organization or project namespace. The `artifactId` identifies the project artifact, and `version` identifies its release version. Compiler properties define the Java release targeted by the build.

A build file may also declare dependencies, plugins, repositories, profiles and packaging behavior. Keep versions controlled and avoid relying on unspecified defaults for important build behavior.

Project metadata is used by developers, IDEs, build servers and artifact repositories. Incorrect coordinates can cause publication collisions or make dependencies difficult to locate. Inconsistent compiler settings can also produce code that builds on one machine but fails on another.

Use source control to track build files and review changes to plugin or dependency versions. CI should build from the committed build definition rather than depending on undocumented settings installed on a developer's machine.

sections.title: Dependencies and External Libraries
sections.content:
# Dependencies and External Libraries

A dependency is an external library or module that a Java project requires to compile, test or run. Examples include logging libraries, JSON serializers, database drivers, testing frameworks and application frameworks.

Maven declares dependencies in `pom.xml`:

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
        <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
        <version>2.0.16</version>
    </dependency>

    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
        <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
        <version>5.11.0</version>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

A dependency is identified by coordinates such as group ID, artifact ID and version. Maven resolves required artifacts from configured repositories and stores downloaded files in its local repository.

Dependency scope determines where a dependency is available. For example, `test` dependencies are used for test compilation and execution rather than normal production compilation. Other scopes have different effects on classpaths and transitive dependency propagation.

A transitive dependency is a library required by another dependency. This can create version conflicts or introduce libraries that the project did not declare directly. Inspect the resolved dependency tree when unexpected behavior occurs:

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
```

Do not add arbitrary JAR files manually to a project without documenting how they are obtained and versioned. Prefer managed dependencies with explicit versions and approved repositories.

In CI/CD, dependency resolution should be repeatable and monitored for known vulnerabilities. Teams should review dependency updates, use trusted repositories and retain enough build information to identify which library versions were included in a released artifact.

sections.title: Compiled Classes, JARs and Build Output
sections.content:
# Compiled Classes, JARs and Build Output

Java build output contains generated files produced during compilation, testing and packaging. In a Maven project, the default output directory is `target`.

A typical build directory may contain:

```text
target/
├── classes/
├── test-classes/
├── surefire-reports/
└── payment-service-1.0.0.jar
```

The `classes` directory contains compiled production classes and copied resources. The `test-classes` directory contains compiled test classes and test resources. Test reports are generated by the configured test plugin. The JAR is the packaged application artifact.

A JAR is an archive containing Java class files, resources and metadata. Inspect its contents with:

```bash
jar --list --file target/payment-service-1.0.0.jar
```

An executable JAR typically has manifest metadata identifying its entry point or framework launcher. Launch behavior depends on how the artifact was packaged:

```bash
java -jar target/payment-service-1.0.0.jar
```

Not every JAR is executable with `java -jar`. A library JAR may have no application entry point and may need to be used as a dependency by another application.

Generated output should normally not be committed to source control. Add build directories such as `target/` to `.gitignore`. The CI pipeline should generate output from the checked-out source and controlled dependencies.

For reliable deployments, publish the artifact produced by the successful build. Record its version and checksum, and promote that same artifact through environments. Do not assume that a JAR with the same filename necessarily contains identical bytes.

sections.title: Multi-Module Java Project Organization
sections.content:
# Multi-Module Java Project Organization

A multi-module Java project separates a larger system into smaller build modules. Each module can own a specific responsibility, dependency set and artifact while sharing a parent build configuration.

A Maven multi-module repository commonly looks like:

```text
payment-platform/
├── pom.xml
├── payment-domain/
│   └── pom.xml
├── payment-service/
│   └── pom.xml
└── payment-api/
    └── pom.xml
```

The root POM can act as an aggregator and list modules:

```xml
<packaging>pom</packaging>

<modules>
    <module>payment-domain</module>
    <module>payment-service</module>
    <module>payment-api</module>
</modules>
```

The domain module may contain core business types. The service module may implement application operations and depend on the domain module. The API module may expose HTTP endpoints and depend on the service module.

A parent POM can centralize shared properties, plugin management and dependency version management. A module POM declares its own artifact coordinates and dependencies. Aggregation and inheritance are related but distinct Maven concepts: an aggregator lists modules to build together, while a parent provides inherited configuration.

Build the project from the root:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Maven calculates the required module build order from inter-module dependencies. If a module depends on another module, the required dependency is built first.

Multi-module design is useful when components have meaningful boundaries and can be tested or reused independently. Avoid splitting a small application into many modules without a clear architectural reason. Excessive module boundaries can increase build complexity and slow down development.

CI pipelines should build the required module set, run relevant tests and publish the correct artifacts. Changes to shared modules may affect downstream modules, so dependency relationships must be understood before release.

sections.title: Project Structure Validation and Troubleshooting
sections.content:
# Project Structure Validation and Troubleshooting

Project structure problems often appear as compilation failures, missing resources, test discovery failures or runtime class-loading errors. Validate the directory layout and build configuration before changing application code.

Start by checking the repository contents and build file:

```bash
mvn validate
mvn test
mvn package
```

The `validate` phase checks basic project information and configuration. `test` compiles and runs tests. `package` creates the configured artifact after the required earlier lifecycle phases.

Common problems include:

- Java source files placed outside configured source roots.
- Package declarations that do not match the intended namespace layout.
- Configuration files stored outside resource directories.
- Test classes placed under production source directories.
- Dependencies missing from the build file.
- Incorrect module declarations in a multi-module project.
- Generated output accidentally committed to source control.
- A main class missing from the executable artifact metadata.

If a resource is missing at runtime, inspect the packaged JAR rather than checking only the source tree:

```bash
jar --list --file target/payment-service-1.0.0.jar
```

If a test is not discovered, verify its source directory, test framework dependency, naming convention and test plugin configuration.

If a module cannot resolve another project module, inspect the root aggregator POM, module paths, artifact coordinates and declared dependencies.

Use a clean build when stale generated output may be hiding a problem:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

A clean build removes previous generated output and rebuilds the project. In CI, build from a fresh checkout where practical and retain test reports and build logs.

A well-structured project makes failures easier to isolate. Validate source roots, resource packaging, module dependencies and artifact contents before concluding that the Java code itself is defective.

Collection Performance, Complexity and Implementation Selection
sections.content:
# Collection Performance, Complexity and Implementation Selection

Collection selection affects application performance because different data structures optimize different operations. Big-O notation describes how operation cost grows as the number of elements increases. It is a useful model, but actual runtime also depends on memory layout, hashing quality, object allocation and workload characteristics.

Typical behavior includes:

| Implementation | Common strengths | Important trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| ArrayList | Fast indexed reads; efficient iteration | Middle insertions and removals shift elements |
| LinkedList | Efficient operations at both ends | Slow indexed access; node memory overhead |
| HashSet | Fast average membership operations | No guaranteed iteration order |
| TreeSet | Sorted elements and range operations | Logarithmic tree operations |
| HashMap | Fast average key lookup | No guaranteed iteration order |
| TreeMap | Sorted keys and range queries | Logarithmic tree operations |
| ArrayDeque | Efficient operations at both ends | Does not permit null elements |

Hash-based operations are commonly constant time on average when hashes are distributed well. Poor hash distribution and collisions can increase work. Tree-based collections typically provide logarithmic lookup, insertion and removal.

For example, checking membership repeatedly in a list may require scanning many elements. A HashSet is usually a better fit when the main requirement is repeated membership testing and ordering is irrelevant.

Benchmark with representative data before optimizing. Include realistic collection sizes, read/write ratios, duplicate rates and object types. Measure allocation and garbage collection effects as well as operation latency.

Avoid assuming one implementation is universally fastest. Select the structure that matches the application's correctness requirements first, then measure performance under realistic conditions.
