sections.content:
# JVM Architecture and the Java Execution Model

The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) is the runtime environment that executes Java bytecode. Java source code is normally compiled by the Java compiler into class files containing bytecode. A compatible JVM implementation loads and executes that bytecode on a supported operating system and hardware platform.

The JVM provides an abstraction between compiled Java programs and the underlying machine. The same compiled application can run on different operating systems when a compatible JVM and required runtime dependencies are available.

A simplified execution flow is:

```text
Java source (.java)
       |
       v
Java compiler (javac)
       |
       v
Bytecode (.class)
       |
       v
Class loading and linking
       |
       v
Runtime memory and execution engine
       |
       v
Operating system and hardware
```

The JVM specification defines the abstract machine behavior, including class-file format, runtime data areas and instruction semantics. Different JVM implementations may use different internal optimizations while respecting the specification.

The JVM should not be confused with the Java Development Kit (JDK) or Java Runtime Environment (JRE). The JDK includes development tools such as `javac` and a runtime. A runtime distribution provides the components needed to execute Java applications, although packaging terminology and distribution contents vary by Java release.

In a production application, JVM behavior affects startup time, memory consumption, garbage collection, thread execution and application latency. Understanding the execution model helps engineers diagnose failures such as class-loading errors, heap exhaustion and excessive garbage collection.

sections.title: Java Compilation, Class Files and Bytecode
sections.content:
# Java Compilation, Class Files and Bytecode

The Java compiler converts Java source code into class files containing JVM bytecode. Bytecode is an instruction format understood by the JVM rather than direct machine instructions for a particular processor.

Compile a Java source file:

```bash
javac HelloApp.java
```

Run the compiled class:

```bash
java HelloApp
```

The compiler checks language syntax and type rules before producing class files. A compilation failure prevents the corresponding output from being generated successfully.

A class file contains more than method instructions. It includes structural information such as the class name, superclass, implemented interfaces, field and method descriptions, attributes and references to other classes. The constant pool stores symbolic information used by the class.

Inspect bytecode using `javap`:

```bash
javap -c -p HelloApp
```

The `-c` option displays bytecode instructions, and `-p` includes private members. This is useful when investigating how a Java expression is compiled or examining compiler-generated methods.

The JVM verifies class-file structure and bytecode constraints during loading and verification. This helps prevent invalid bytecode from being executed as if it were valid code.

Build tools such as Maven and Gradle compile source files and package class files into JAR artifacts. A JAR is a packaging format; it does not itself execute Java instructions. The JVM loads classes from the JAR through class-loading mechanisms.

For production debugging, inspect the exact artifact deployed to the environment. Source code in a repository may differ from the class files actually running because of stale builds, dependency differences or incorrect deployment artifacts.

sections.title: Class Loading, Linking and Initialization Lifecycle
Class Loader Architecture and Parent Delegation
sections.content:
# Class Loader Architecture and Parent Delegation

A class loader is responsible for locating and defining class files for the JVM. Java uses a class-loader hierarchy so that core runtime classes and application classes can be loaded through different mechanisms.

Common built-in loaders include:

- Bootstrap class loader: loads core platform classes. Its implementation is commonly native or otherwise represented specially by the JVM.
- Platform class loader: loads platform classes and modules beyond the core bootstrap set.
- Application class loader: loads application classes from the configured class path or module path.

The standard delegation approach asks a parent loader to load a class before the child loader attempts to define it. This helps prevent application code from accidentally replacing core platform classes with classes of the same name.

A class is identified by both its binary name and its defining class loader. Two classes with the same fully qualified name but different defining loaders are different runtime types and may not be assignment-compatible.

Custom class loaders are useful in plugin systems, application servers, modular runtimes and environments that isolate dependencies. They must be designed carefully because class identity and visibility depend on loader relationships.

ClassNotFoundException generally means an explicit class-loading request could not locate a class. NoClassDefFoundError generally indicates that a class definition needed during execution is unavailable or could not be initialized successfully.

Useful diagnostic commands include:

```bash
java -Xlog:class+load=info -jar application.jar
```

Class-loading logs can reveal where classes are loaded from and help investigate duplicate libraries, incompatible dependencies and unexpected class-loader boundaries.

sections.title: JVM Runtime Data Areas and Memory Organization
sections.content:
# JVM Runtime Data Areas and Memory Organization

The JVM defines runtime data areas that store information required during execution. Some areas are shared among threads, while others are associated with individual threads.

The main runtime data areas include:

- Heap: stores class instances and arrays.
- Java virtual machine stacks: maintain method invocation frames for individual threads.
- Program counters: track the current JVM instruction for each thread executing Java code.
- Native method stacks: support native method execution where required by the JVM implementation.
- Method area: stores per-class structures such as runtime constant pools, field and method information, and method code.

The JVM specification describes logical runtime areas. It does not require every implementation to organize physical memory in exactly the same way.

For example, the heap is shared by threads, so objects can be referenced from different threads. This creates concurrency concerns when mutable objects are shared. Thread-local stacks hold invocation frames and local execution state for each thread.

A common diagnostic mistake is to treat every memory problem as a heap problem. A Java process can fail because of native memory exhaustion, excessive thread creation, direct-buffer usage or class metadata pressure even when the Java heap has free space.

Memory investigations should therefore include heap metrics, thread counts, garbage collection logs, native memory tracking where enabled and operating-system process memory.

Understanding which runtime area owns a resource narrows the diagnosis. Heap dumps help inspect Java object retention, while thread dumps help investigate thread states, blocked execution and excessive thread creation.

sections.title: Heap Memory, Object Allocation and Reachability
Java Stack Frames, Method Calls and Local Variables
Method Area, Metaspace and Runtime Class Metadata
sections.content:
# Method Area, Metaspace and Runtime Class Metadata

The JVM specification defines a logical method area that stores per-class structures such as runtime constant pools, field and method data, and method code. It is shared among threads.

HotSpot JVM uses Metaspace to store class metadata. Metaspace is native memory rather than part of the ordinary Java object heap. This distinction matters when diagnosing memory pressure.

Class metadata is created as classes are loaded and can be reclaimed when the defining class loader and its classes become eligible for unloading, subject to JVM conditions. If an application continuously creates class loaders or prevents them from being reclaimed, metadata usage can grow.

A common cause of class-loader-related memory leaks is retaining references to application classes through static fields, thread-local values or long-lived threads owned by a parent class loader.

Metaspace can be limited with:

```bash
java -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m -jar application.jar
```

This setting should not be applied blindly. A limit that is too small can cause OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace even when the Java heap has sufficient capacity.

Useful investigation commands include:

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.classloader_stats
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
```

The first command can show class-loader statistics on supported JVMs. The second can help inspect object counts and memory usage, although it may have operational impact on a busy process.

In containerized production systems, track both JVM heap and total process memory. Native metadata, thread stacks and other native allocations contribute to the container's memory usage and can cause an out-of-memory termination outside the Java heap.

sections.title: Execution Engine, Interpreter and JIT Compilation
sections.content:
# Execution Engine, Interpreter and JIT Compilation

The JVM execution engine executes bytecode. JVM implementations may interpret bytecode, compile frequently executed code into native machine instructions or combine both approaches.

An interpreter executes bytecode instructions as the program runs. This allows classes to begin executing without first compiling every method into optimized machine code.

A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler identifies code that executes frequently and compiles selected methods or code paths into native instructions. HotSpot uses profiling information and compilation tiers to optimize frequently executed code.

The JVM can apply optimizations such as method inlining, dead-code elimination and loop optimizations when it can preserve Java program semantics. Optimized code may be deoptimized if runtime assumptions become invalid.

This means application performance can change after startup. A short benchmark may measure interpreter or early compilation behavior, while a longer-running service may reach a more optimized execution state.

Inspect compilation activity with supported JVM diagnostic options:

```bash
java -XX:+PrintCompilation -jar application.jar
```

Option availability and output behavior depend on the Java release and JVM implementation. For unified JVM logging, consult the options supported by the deployed runtime.

Do not assume that manually forcing compilation or changing JIT flags will automatically improve production performance. First measure CPU usage, allocation rate, garbage collection pauses and application latency.

For reliable performance testing, use representative workloads, warm-up periods and repeated measurements. Benchmark frameworks such as JMH are designed to reduce common errors in Java microbenchmarks.

sections.title: Garbage Collection Interaction with JVM Runtime
sections.content:
# Garbage Collection Interaction with JVM Runtime

Garbage collection reclaims heap memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable according to the collector's liveness analysis. It reduces the need for application code to manually free ordinary Java objects.

A collector identifies live objects by tracing references from GC roots. Roots can include references from active thread stacks, static fields and JVM-managed structures. Objects reachable from these roots are retained.

Different garbage collectors use different algorithms and trade-offs. They may divide the heap into regions or generations, perform concurrent marking, compact memory or use other strategies.

The choice of collector affects throughput, pause times, CPU usage and memory footprint. There is no universally best collector for every application.

Useful runtime flags include:

```bash
java -Xlog:gc* -jar application.jar
```

Unified logging can report collection events and memory behavior on modern Java releases. The exact log details depend on the JVM version and collector.

A garbage collection event is not automatically evidence of a memory leak. A healthy application can allocate many short-lived objects and collect them frequently. More concerning patterns include steadily rising post-collection occupancy, repeated full collections and long pauses that affect service latency.

In production, correlate GC logs with request latency, CPU utilization, allocation rate and container memory. Investigate whether the problem is excessive allocation, retained objects, insufficient heap sizing or a collector configuration mismatch.

Do not use `System.gc()` as a normal memory-management strategy. It requests garbage collection behavior but does not guarantee that a collection will occur immediately.

sections.title: Native Methods, JNI and Direct Memory
sections.content:
# Native Methods, JNI and Direct Memory

Java applications can interact with native code through the Java Native Interface (JNI). Native methods are implemented outside ordinary Java bytecode and can call platform-specific libraries.

JNI is used in cases such as operating-system integration, hardware access, specialized libraries and performance-sensitive components. Native code introduces additional responsibilities because memory safety and resource handling are no longer managed entirely by the Java language.

Java applications also use memory outside the ordinary Java heap. Examples include direct byte buffers, native library allocations, thread stacks and JVM internal structures.

A direct byte buffer can be created with:

```java
import java.nio.ByteBuffer;

ByteBuffer buffer = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1024 * 1024);
```

Direct buffers can be useful for certain I/O workloads because they provide memory outside the normal Java heap. They have different allocation and cleanup characteristics from ordinary heap-backed arrays.

A Java process can consume substantially more memory than its configured `-Xmx` heap limit. If a container has a strict memory limit, native memory usage must be considered alongside heap usage.

Native Memory Tracking can be enabled on supported HotSpot JVMs:

```bash
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar application.jar
```

Then inspect memory categories with:

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
```

Native Memory Tracking has overhead and must be enabled at startup. It does not account for every possible external native allocation.

When diagnosing container memory termination, compare JVM heap metrics, native memory tracking, thread count, direct buffer usage and operating-system process memory rather than assuming that `-Xmx` represents the total memory footprint.

sections.title: JVM Threads, Synchronization and Runtime Coordination
JVM Monitoring, Diagnostic Commands and Runtime Observability
sections.content:
# JVM Monitoring, Diagnostic Commands and Runtime Observability

JVM monitoring provides evidence about application memory, threads, garbage collection, class loading and runtime performance. Diagnosis should begin with the symptoms and the exact Java process rather than changing JVM flags without evidence.

Find the process ID and inspect supported runtime details:

```bash
jcmd -l
jcmd <pid> VM.version
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
```

Useful commands include:

- `jcmd`: sends diagnostic commands to a running JVM.
- `jstack` or `jcmd Thread.print`: captures thread information.
- `jstat`: displays selected JVM statistics.
- `jmap`: provides heap-related diagnostic operations.
- `jfr`: works with Java Flight Recorder recordings.
- `jconsole` and VisualVM: provide graphical monitoring capabilities.

Create a heap dump when investigating suspected object retention:

```bash
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/application-heap.hprof
```

Heap dumps can be large and may briefly affect the process. They can contain sensitive application data, so store them securely and control access.

Java Flight Recorder can capture runtime events such as allocation activity, thread behavior and execution samples:

```bash
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diagnostic settings=profile
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=diagnostic filename=/tmp/diagnostic.jfr
```

Command availability and syntax vary by Java version and JVM distribution. Verify the installed runtime's supported options before using them in production.

Correlate JVM metrics with application-level indicators such as request rate, error rate and latency. A useful diagnosis connects runtime evidence to user-visible impact rather than treating an isolated GC event or high heap percentage as proof of a problem.

sections.title: JVM Production Diagnostics and Hands-On Runtime Investigation
sections.content:
# JVM Production Diagnostics and Hands-On Runtime Investigation

This lab investigates a Java service using JVM diagnostic commands and runtime evidence.

First, identify the running JVM:

```bash
jcmd -l
```

Inspect its version and startup configuration:

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.version
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
```

Enable or inspect garbage collection logging using the options appropriate for the Java version. On modern Java releases, unified logging can be configured at startup:

```bash
java -Xlog:gc*:file=/tmp/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar application.jar
```

If the service is already running, inspect its thread state:

```bash
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
```

Look for blocked threads, long-running operations, deadlock reports and unexpectedly large thread counts. A thread dump is a snapshot, so collect multiple samples when investigating intermittent behavior.

For a suspected memory-retention problem, capture a heap dump:

```bash
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/service-heap.hprof
```

Analyze the dump with a suitable heap-analysis tool. Look for large retained object graphs, unexpectedly growing collections, static references and objects held by long-lived listeners or caches.

For CPU investigations, use Java Flight Recorder or another approved profiler to identify hot methods, allocation-heavy code and lock contention. Compare observations with application latency and CPU metrics.

A practical investigation sequence is:

1. Record the Java version, JVM flags and container memory limit.
2. Capture heap, process memory, CPU and thread-count metrics.
3. Inspect GC logs for allocation pressure and post-collection occupancy.
4. Capture thread dumps when latency or blocked execution is observed.
5. Capture a heap dump only when object retention needs investigation.
6. Correlate findings with application traffic and recent deployments.
7. Test a targeted correction in a controlled environment before production rollout.

Heap dumps and recordings can contain confidential information. Protect them with appropriate access controls and retention policies. Avoid expensive diagnostic operations during a critical incident unless the expected evidence justifies their impact.

sections.title: Java Memory Management Model and Object Lifecycle
Object Allocation, References and Heap Utilization
sections.content:
# Object Allocation, References and Heap Utilization

Most Java class instances and arrays are allocated from the JVM heap. The heap is shared among application threads, and the JVM uses an allocation strategy appropriate to its garbage collector and runtime implementation.

Object allocation can occur frequently in normal application code. Creating request objects, collections, strings, response models and temporary calculation objects all contribute to allocation activity.

```java
List<String> deploymentNames = new ArrayList<>();

deploymentNames.add("api-service");
deploymentNames.add("worker-service");

Deployment deployment = new Deployment("release-2026");
```

Each object has a lifetime determined by the references that keep it reachable. A local variable can hold a reference, an object field can refer to another object, and a static field can retain an object for a long time.

An object graph describes these relationships. If a long-lived object refers to a large collection, and that collection refers to many other objects, the entire reachable graph may remain in memory.

The JVM may optimize allocation internally. For example, some objects may be eliminated or have their allocations optimized when the JIT compiler proves that doing so preserves program behavior. Therefore, source-level object creation does not always translate directly into a physical heap allocation.

Monitor both current heap occupancy and allocation rate. A service can have a high allocation rate but low retained memory if most objects are short-lived. Another service can have a modest allocation rate but steadily increasing retained memory because objects remain referenced.

Use representative load tests to understand allocation behavior. Optimize unnecessary object creation only after profiling identifies it as a meaningful contributor to CPU, memory or garbage collection pressure.

sections.title: Garbage Collection Roots and Object Reachability
Heap Generations, Young Collection and Old Collection
sections.content:
# Heap Generations, Young Collection and Old Collection

Many garbage collectors organize heap management around the observation that a large proportion of newly created objects become unreachable quickly. Generational collectors use different regions or generations to manage objects according to their age and survival behavior.

In traditional generational terminology:

- Young generation: receives many newly allocated objects.
- Eden area: commonly the initial allocation region for young objects.
- Survivor areas: hold objects that survive young collections.
- Old generation: holds objects that survive long enough to be promoted or are allocated there under collector-specific rules.

A young collection reclaims unreachable objects in the young generation. Surviving objects may be copied or promoted according to the collector's policy.

An old-generation collection handles objects in the older part of the heap. Depending on the collector, it may involve concurrent marking, compaction or other operations.

The exact physical organization and terminology vary by garbage collector. G1, for example, manages the heap as regions rather than requiring developers to think only in terms of one fixed contiguous young area and one fixed contiguous old area.

Generational collection can improve efficiency when short-lived objects dominate. However, applications that retain many objects or allocate large objects can behave differently.

A common diagnostic clue is repeated growth in old-generation occupancy after collections. It may indicate retained objects, a cache that grows without bounds or an unexpectedly long object lifetime.

Do not assume every old-generation increase is a leak. Compare occupancy after collection over time, inspect heap dumps when justified and correlate memory behavior with workload changes.

sections.title: Garbage Collection Algorithms and Collector Trade-Offs
sections.content:
# Garbage Collection Algorithms and Collector Trade-Offs

Garbage collectors use algorithms to identify unreachable objects and reclaim their memory. Different algorithms make different trade-offs among throughput, pause duration, CPU consumption, memory overhead and predictability.

Common algorithmic techniques include:

- Marking: identifies objects that remain reachable.
- Sweeping: reclaims storage belonging to objects that are not live.
- Copying: moves live objects into another memory region and reclaims the source region.
- Compaction: moves live objects together to reduce fragmentation.
- Concurrent collection: performs selected collection work while application threads continue executing.
- Parallel collection: uses multiple worker threads to perform collection work.

A collector may combine several techniques. For example, it can perform parallel work during stop-the-world pauses and concurrent work while application threads are running.

Stop-the-world means application threads are paused for a particular garbage collection phase. Such pauses are not automatically failures, but long pauses can increase request latency and cause missed response-time objectives.

Throughput measures how much application work is completed relative to time spent on garbage collection. Latency-sensitive services may prefer shorter pauses even when that requires more CPU or memory overhead.

No collector is best for every workload. A batch-processing job may prioritize throughput, while a user-facing API may prioritize predictable response latency.

Select a collector based on measurements from representative traffic. Compare pause distributions, CPU utilization, allocation rate, heap occupancy and application response times. Avoid choosing a collector solely because it is popular or because one benchmark reported favorable results.

sections.title: G1 Garbage Collector and Region-Based Heap Management
sections.content:
# G1 Garbage Collector and Region-Based Heap Management

G1, or Garbage-First Garbage Collector, is a region-based collector designed to balance throughput and pause-time goals. It divides the heap into regions and selects collection work based partly on the amount of reclaimable space and collection cost.

Unlike a simple fixed contiguous young and old heap layout, G1 can use regions for different roles over time. Eden, survivor and old regions are logical roles assigned to heap regions.

G1 commonly performs young collections and may perform mixed collections that include selected old regions. Its concurrent marking process helps determine which old regions contain reclaimable space.

Enable G1 explicitly when required:

```bash
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xms1g -Xmx2g -jar application.jar
```

The exact default collector depends on the Java release, vendor and runtime configuration. Verify the collector actually selected by the running JVM rather than assuming the command-line default.

A pause-time target can be supplied as a tuning goal:

```bash
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200
```

This is a target used by the collector's heuristics, not a hard guarantee that every pause will remain below 200 milliseconds.

G1 is useful for many server workloads, but it still requires adequate heap capacity and a reasonable allocation profile. Large object allocation, high retained memory and excessive allocation rates can create pressure.

Inspect GC logs to understand young collection frequency, mixed collection behavior, pause duration and concurrent marking. Tune only after identifying which behavior is affecting the service.

In a production environment, validate changes under representative load and compare latency percentiles, CPU consumption and memory usage before and after the change.

sections.title: Low-Latency Collectors and Z Garbage Collector
sections.content:
# Low-Latency Collectors and Z Garbage Collector

Some applications require very short garbage collection pauses because long pauses can disrupt interactive requests, streaming operations or latency-sensitive services.

The Z Garbage Collector (ZGC) is a low-latency garbage collector designed to perform much of its work concurrently with application execution. Its design aims to keep pause times short while managing large heaps.

Enable ZGC on a Java release that supports the required collector mode:

```bash
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms2g -Xmx4g -jar application.jar
```

Collector availability and supported options vary by Java release and distribution. Newer releases may provide additional ZGC modes or different option behavior, so check the deployed JDK documentation.

Concurrent collection does not mean that application threads are never paused. ZGC still has synchronization points and runtime phases that require pauses, but its design aims to minimize their duration.

A low-pause collector may consume additional CPU or memory resources to achieve its latency characteristics. A workload with limited CPU capacity may not benefit if concurrent collection competes heavily with application threads.

Evaluate whether the service actually has a garbage-collection latency problem before switching collectors. High request latency can also result from slow database calls, network delays, lock contention or overloaded application threads.

Compare pause-time percentiles, application latency, CPU consumption, allocation rate and memory headroom under the same workload. The correct collector is the one that meets the service's operational requirements with acceptable resource cost.

sections.title: Memory Leaks, Retained Objects and Reference Management
sections.content:
# Memory Leaks, Retained Objects and Reference Management

A Java memory leak occurs when objects remain reachable even though the application no longer needs them. The garbage collector cannot reclaim those objects because a live reference still exists.

Typical causes include:

- Unbounded application caches.
- Static collections that continually accumulate entries.
- Event listeners that are registered but never removed.
- Thread-local values retained by long-lived worker threads.
- Queues that receive data faster than consumers process it.
- Session or request data retained beyond its intended lifetime.

For example:

```java
class RequestHistory {
    private static final List<String> REQUESTS = new ArrayList<>();

    static void record(String requestId) {
        REQUESTS.add(requestId);
    }
}
```

This static list grows continuously unless entries are removed or the application is restarted. A high-volume service can eventually exhaust its heap.

Use bounded caches with explicit size or expiration policies. Remove listeners when their owners are destroyed. Clear thread-local state when work completes, particularly when using pooled threads. Apply backpressure or bounded queues when producers can outpace consumers.

A rising heap graph alone does not prove a leak. The application may be warming a cache or processing a larger workload. A stronger indicator is a persistent increase in post-collection retained memory under comparable workload conditions.

Heap dumps can reveal dominator objects, retained sizes and paths to GC roots. Compare dumps from different times when practical to identify which object groups continue growing.

Fix the ownership or lifecycle problem that retains objects. Increasing `-Xmx` can delay an out-of-memory failure, but it does not remove an unbounded retention path.

sections.title: OutOfMemoryError Types and JVM Memory Exhaustion
sections.content:
# OutOfMemoryError Types and JVM Memory Exhaustion

OutOfMemoryError indicates that the JVM or a related runtime allocation could not obtain the required memory. It does not always mean that the Java heap is full.

Important failure categories include:

- `Java heap space`: the JVM could not allocate an object in the heap.
- `GC overhead limit exceeded`: the JVM spent a very high proportion of time collecting while recovering very little heap space, when this protection is enabled.
- `Metaspace`: class metadata allocation could not obtain sufficient native memory or exceeded a configured limit.
- `Direct buffer memory`: direct buffer allocation could not obtain sufficient capacity.
- `unable to create native thread`: the process or operating system could not create another thread.

The message helps identify the affected resource, but investigation still requires runtime and operating-system evidence.

For heap exhaustion, inspect heap occupancy, allocation patterns and retained object graphs. For Metaspace exhaustion, investigate class loading and class-loader retention. For native-thread failures, inspect thread counts, stack-size settings and operating-system process limits.

A heap dump can be requested automatically when heap exhaustion occurs:

```bash
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError
-XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/log/java
```

Ensure the configured location has sufficient disk space and appropriate access controls. Heap dumps may contain confidential data.

Do not treat every OutOfMemoryError by immediately increasing heap size. The container may have a smaller memory limit than the requested heap, or the failure may originate in native memory.

The correct response is to identify the resource that failed, preserve useful evidence and determine whether the cause is a leak, workload spike, incorrect sizing, excessive thread creation or another runtime constraint.

sections.title: Heap Dumps, Heap Analysis and Memory Profiling
sections.content:
# Heap Dumps, Heap Analysis and Memory Profiling

A heap dump is a snapshot of objects and reference relationships in the Java heap. It helps investigate retained memory, large collections and object graphs that may explain heap exhaustion.

A heap dump can be generated from a running JVM using:

```bash
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/application.hprof
```

The operation may affect application performance and can require significant disk space. Schedule or perform it with awareness of production impact.

Analyze the dump with a heap-analysis tool. Useful views include:

- Histogram of classes and object counts.
- Shallow size of individual objects.
- Retained size of object graphs.
- Dominator tree showing objects that retain large portions of memory.
- Paths to GC roots explaining why objects remain reachable.

Shallow size is the memory occupied by an object itself. Retained size estimates the memory that would become reclaimable if that object and the objects retained exclusively through it were removed.

A class histogram can provide a quicker overview:

```bash
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
```

The command can be expensive for a large process, so use it carefully during an incident.

Profilers can also reveal allocation hotspots, object lifetime patterns and methods that allocate large numbers of objects. Allocation profiling is particularly useful when high garbage collection activity is caused by temporary object creation rather than a leak.

Heap dumps, profiler recordings and histograms can expose user data, tokens or other confidential information. Store them securely, restrict access and remove them according to operational retention policies.

sections.title: Garbage Collection Logging and JVM Memory Diagnostics
sections.content:
# Garbage Collection Logging and JVM Memory Diagnostics

Garbage collection logs provide evidence about collection frequency, pause duration, heap occupancy and collector behavior. They are essential for understanding whether memory pressure is affecting application performance.

On modern Java releases, unified JVM logging can be enabled with:

```bash
java -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/java/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags -jar application.jar
```

The `gc*` selector includes garbage collection-related log tags. The file output allows operators to retain logs for analysis, subject to appropriate rotation and disk management.

Older Java releases used different logging flags. Do not copy GC logging options between Java versions without verifying compatibility.

Useful runtime inspection commands include:

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
```

The exact commands available depend on the JVM implementation and version.

Review these indicators together:

- Heap occupancy before and after collection.
- Young and old collection frequency.
- Pause duration and distribution.
- Allocation rate.
- Time spent in concurrent collection phases.
- Metaspace and direct-memory behavior.
- Thread count and process memory.

A single long pause does not establish a permanent collector problem. Investigate whether the pause is repeated, whether it correlates with latency spikes and whether the application was under unusual load.

Build a timeline that combines GC logs with application request latency, CPU utilization, container memory and deployment events. This helps distinguish memory-related symptoms from database, network or application-level delays.

sections.title: JVM Memory Sizing, Container Limits and Production Tuning
sections.content:
# JVM Memory Sizing, Container Limits and Production Tuning

JVM memory sizing must account for more than the Java heap. The total process footprint can include heap, Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, JIT code cache, native libraries and other native allocations.

For example:

```bash
java -Xms512m -Xmx2g -jar application.jar
```

This configures the initial and maximum heap sizing targets. It does not reserve or cap every byte used by the process.

In a container, the memory limit applies to the container's total memory consumption, not just the Java heap. If the heap maximum is set too close to the container limit, native allocations and operating-system overhead can push the process beyond its available memory.

Modern JVMs can recognize container resource constraints, but behavior depends on Java version, vendor and configuration. Inspect the actual JVM flags and runtime ergonomics rather than assuming container awareness is configured correctly.

A production sizing process should:

1. Measure steady-state and peak heap occupancy.
2. Measure total process memory under representative load.
3. Include headroom for native memory, thread stacks and runtime structures.
4. Observe allocation rate and garbage collection behavior.
5. Test startup, peak traffic and failure scenarios.
6. Validate the result against the container or host memory limit.

Avoid setting `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx` automatically without considering deployment constraints. Fixed sizing may be appropriate in some environments, but it should be a deliberate operational choice.

When tuning, change one meaningful variable at a time and compare the same workload. Record the Java version, collector, heap settings and container limits so that the result can be reproduced across environments.

sections.title: Production Memory Incident Investigation and Recovery Lab
sections.content:
# Production Memory Incident Investigation and Recovery Lab

This lab follows a structured investigation of a Java service whose container memory usage is increasing and whose requests are becoming slower.

Start by recording the environment:

```bash
java -version
jcmd -l
```

Identify the service process and inspect its runtime configuration:

```bash
jcmd <pid> VM.version
jcmd <pid> VM.flags
jcmd <pid> VM.command_line
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info
```

Next, compare Java heap metrics with total container memory. If heap usage is stable but container memory continues to rise, investigate native memory, thread stacks, direct buffers and other process allocations.

Inspect garbage collection logs for repeated full collections, long pauses and increasing post-collection occupancy. If the heap retains more data after each collection under comparable load, capture a heap dump when operationally safe.

```bash
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/incident-heap.hprof
```

Analyze the dump for large retained object graphs and paths to GC roots. Check whether caches, static collections, listeners, thread-local values or queues retain objects unexpectedly.

Capture thread information if thread counts or native memory are increasing:

```bash
jcmd <pid> Thread.print
```

Review recent code changes, traffic growth, configuration changes and deployment differences. A new cache policy or an unbounded queue can create memory growth even when the JVM configuration has not changed.

Possible corrective actions include bounding caches, removing stale references, limiting concurrency, applying backpressure, fixing resource ownership or adjusting memory sizing after measuring the actual footprint.

After applying a correction, repeat the same load test and compare heap occupancy, post-GC memory, allocation rate, pause times, container memory and request latency.

Do not restart the service before collecting useful evidence unless immediate recovery is required. If a restart is necessary to restore availability, preserve available logs and metrics first when practical. Treat heap dumps and diagnostic recordings as sensitive production artifacts.

sections.title: Maven Build Automation and Project Integration
sections.content:
# Maven Build Automation and Project Integration

Apache Maven is a build automation and dependency management tool commonly used for Java applications. It provides a consistent project model, a standard directory structure, dependency resolution and a lifecycle for compiling, testing, packaging and deploying software.

Maven describes a project through its Project Object Model, stored in a `pom.xml` file. This file defines project identity, dependencies, plugins, build configuration and relationships with other Maven projects.

A developer can build a Maven project with:

```bash
mvn clean package
```

This command asks Maven to execute lifecycle phases through `package`. The resulting artifact may be a JAR or WAR depending on the project packaging configuration.

Maven integrates with IDEs, local development environments, CI servers and artifact repositories. A CI pipeline can use the same Maven project definition that developers use locally, reducing differences between build environments.

Maven does not automatically guarantee reproducible or secure builds. Build results still depend on dependency versions, plugin versions, repository contents, JDK versions and external configuration.

A reliable integration defines the required JDK, pins important plugin versions, manages dependencies deliberately and verifies the produced artifact.

In a DevOps workflow, Maven typically sits between source checkout and artifact publication. The pipeline checks out code, resolves dependencies, compiles sources, runs tests, packages the application and publishes the versioned artifact for later deployment.

sections.title: Maven Project Directory Structure and Standard Conventions
sections.content:
# Maven Project Directory Structure and Standard Conventions

Maven encourages a standard directory layout so developers and build tools can understand a project without extensive custom configuration.

A typical Java application uses this structure:

```text
my-application/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/
│   │   └── resources/
│   └── test/
│       ├── java/
│       └── resources/
└── target/
```

`src/main/java` contains production Java source files. `src/main/resources` contains application resources such as configuration files and templates.

`src/test/java` contains test source files, while `src/test/resources` contains resources used by tests.

The `target` directory is generated during builds. It can contain compiled classes, processed resources, test reports, packaged artifacts and other intermediate output. It should normally not be committed to source control.

The standard layout allows Maven's default plugins to locate source files and resources without custom directory declarations.

Create a project from an archetype when a suitable starter template is available:

```bash
mvn archetype:generate
```

An archetype generates an initial project structure, but its output should be reviewed before use.

For a Spring Boot application, Java packages commonly separate controllers, services, repositories, configuration and domain models. Maven manages the build layout; the application's package architecture remains an application design decision.

Keep source files, test files and generated build output separate. This makes builds easier to understand, review and reproduce across developer machines and CI agents.

sections.title: POM XML Structure and Project Coordinates
sections.content:
# POM XML Structure and Project Coordinates

The Project Object Model, or POM, is Maven's central project configuration file. It is normally named `pom.xml` and written in XML.

A basic POM defines the project coordinates and packaging:

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0
         https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">

    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>deployment-service</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>
</project>
```

The three main coordinates are:

- `groupId`: identifies the organization or logical project group.
- `artifactId`: identifies the specific project or artifact.
- `version`: identifies the release or development version.

Together, these coordinates identify a Maven artifact. A dependency can reference another artifact using the same coordinates.

The `packaging` element determines the primary artifact type, commonly `jar`, `war` or `pom`. If omitted, Maven uses `jar` as the default packaging.

Other important POM elements include `properties`, `dependencies`, `dependencyManagement`, `build`, `repositories`, `pluginManagement` and `modules`.

Maven also constructs an effective POM by combining the project's configuration with inherited parent configuration and applicable profiles. Inspect it when a build behaves differently from what the local POM appears to specify:

```bash
mvn help:effective-pom
```

Understanding the effective POM is important when parent POMs or shared build conventions introduce configuration that is not visible directly in the current project file.

sections.title: Dependency Management, Transitive Dependencies and Version Control
sections.content:
# Dependency Management, Transitive Dependencies and Version Control

Maven dependencies allow a project to reuse external libraries without manually downloading and copying JAR files into the source repository.

A dependency is declared in the POM:

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        <version>6.2.0</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Maven resolves the declared artifact and its required transitive dependencies. A transitive dependency is a library required by another library in the dependency graph.

This graph can contain multiple versions of the same library. Maven uses dependency mediation rules to select versions, and the resulting selection should be inspected when compatibility issues occur.

Useful commands include:

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
mvn dependency:analyze
```

The dependency tree displays the resolved dependency hierarchy. Dependency analysis can identify declared dependencies that appear unused or used dependencies that are not directly declared, although its results require review.

For applications with several modules, `dependencyManagement` can centralize dependency versions:

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-bom</artifactId>
            <version>5.11.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
```

A managed version is applied when a matching dependency is declared without its own version. Dependency management does not automatically add that dependency to the project.

Use deliberate version policies, review dependency updates and check for known vulnerabilities. Avoid uncontrolled version ranges in production builds because they can cause different builds to resolve different dependency versions over time.

sections.title: Dependency Scopes and Classpath Behavior
sections.content:
# Dependency Scopes and Classpath Behavior

Maven dependency scopes determine where a dependency is available during the build and whether it is included in the resulting artifact's runtime dependency requirements.

Common scopes include:

- `compile`: available on the main compilation and test classpaths; this is the default scope.
- `provided`: required for compilation and tests but expected to be supplied by the runtime environment.
- `runtime`: not required to compile main source code but required when the application runs.
- `test`: available only for test compilation and test execution.
- `system`: references a local filesystem artifact and is generally discouraged because it harms portability.

Example:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

The testing dependency is available to test code without becoming a normal application runtime dependency.

A `provided` dependency is appropriate when the deployment environment supplies the required library, such as certain servlet APIs in a managed application server. It should not be used when the packaged application must provide that library itself.

Scope also affects transitive dependency propagation. Maven applies different rules when one project depends on another project with a particular scope.

Incorrect scope selection can create failures that appear only at runtime. For example, an application may compile successfully but fail with `ClassNotFoundException` if a required runtime library is missing from the deployed classpath.

Inspect the dependency tree and packaged artifact when diagnosing classpath problems. Verify that the actual deployment environment provides every library intentionally excluded from the application's package.

sections.title: Maven Build Lifecycle, Phases and Goals
sections.content:
# Maven Build Lifecycle, Phases and Goals

Maven organizes build operations into lifecycles. A lifecycle is a sequence of phases, and each phase can execute one or more plugin goals.

The three built-in lifecycles are:

- `default`: handles project validation, compilation, testing, packaging and deployment-related build operations.
- `clean`: removes generated build output.
- `site`: generates project documentation and reports.

Important phases in the default lifecycle include:

```text
validate
compile
test
package
verify
install
deploy
```

Invoking a later phase executes the preceding phases in that lifecycle. For example:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Maven first executes the clean lifecycle's `clean` phase and then executes the default lifecycle through `verify`.

The difference between a phase and a goal is important. A phase is a lifecycle stage, while a goal is a specific operation provided by a plugin.

For example, the compiler plugin provides goals that compile source code. Maven binds plugin goals to lifecycle phases according to the project's packaging and plugin configuration.

You can also invoke a plugin goal directly:

```bash
mvn compiler:compile
```

Direct goal invocation is useful for targeted operations, but it does not necessarily execute all earlier lifecycle phases.

For CI pipelines, choose lifecycle commands that express the intended quality gate. `package` creates the artifact, while `verify` runs additional verification steps bound to the lifecycle. Use `install` when the artifact must be placed in the local repository, and `deploy` when the configured distribution process should publish it to a remote repository.

sections.title: Maven Plugins, Compiler Configuration and Build Customization
sections.content:
# Maven Plugins, Compiler Configuration and Build Customization

Maven plugins implement build operations such as compiling Java code, running tests, creating JAR files, generating reports and publishing artifacts.

A plugin is configured in the POM. For example, the compiler plugin controls Java source and target compilation settings.

```xml
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <version>3.13.0</version>
            <configuration>
                <release>17</release>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

The `release` option tells the compiler to compile against the specified Java platform API and language level. The JDK used to execute Maven must also be compatible with the selected release.

Other common plugins include:

- Maven Surefire Plugin for unit test execution.
- Maven Failsafe Plugin for integration test execution.
- Maven Jar Plugin for JAR packaging.
- Maven War Plugin for WAR packaging.
- Maven Resources Plugin for resource processing.
- Maven Checkstyle Plugin for configured code style checks.

Pin plugin versions so that builds do not unexpectedly change when plugin defaults or metadata change.

`pluginManagement` centralizes plugin versions and configuration, especially in parent POMs. It does not by itself execute every managed plugin. A plugin generally needs to be declared in the appropriate build configuration to participate in the project build.

When a build behaves unexpectedly, inspect the effective POM and Maven debug output:

```bash
mvn -X package
```

Debug output can reveal plugin configuration and resolution details, but it may contain environment information. Review it before sharing logs publicly.

sections.title: Repositories, Local Cache and Artifact Resolution
sections.content:
# Repositories, Local Cache and Artifact Resolution

Maven repositories store project artifacts such as libraries, plugin binaries, parent POMs and packaged application releases.

Maven commonly interacts with three repository locations:

- Local repository: a cache on the developer or CI machine.
- Remote repositories: servers from which Maven downloads artifacts.
- Deployment repositories: destinations where authorized builds publish artifacts.

The default local repository is commonly under the user's home directory in `.m2/repository`. It can be inspected with:

```bash
mvn help:evaluate -Dexpression=settings.localRepository -q -DforceStdout
```

When Maven resolves a dependency, it checks the local repository and uses configured remote repositories when necessary.

Repository configuration can be defined in project POMs or user and global settings. Credentials should be stored in Maven settings rather than committed into a project POM.

Example repository server configuration:

```xml
<servers>
    <server>
        <id>internal-releases</id>
        <username>${env.MAVEN_REPO_USER}</username>
        <password>${env.MAVEN_REPO_PASSWORD}</password>
    </server>
</servers>
```

The server ID must match the repository or distribution-management ID used by the build configuration.

A cached artifact can make a build succeed even when a remote repository is temporarily unavailable. A clean CI agent may expose the underlying repository or credential problem because it has no existing cache.

For reliable builds, use approved repository managers, protect credentials, control artifact retention and avoid depending on mutable release artifacts. Snapshot dependencies are intended for ongoing development and can change as new snapshots are published.

sections.title: Multi-Module Maven Projects and Parent POM Architecture
sections.content:
# Multi-Module Maven Projects and Parent POM Architecture

A multi-module Maven project builds several related projects from a shared parent or aggregator POM. This is useful when an application is divided into independently organized modules that share build conventions.

A root POM can declare modules:

```xml
<project>
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>platform</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <modules>
        <module>common</module>
        <module>service</module>
        <module>web</module>
    </modules>
</project>
```

Each module normally has its own `pom.xml`. A module can depend on another module using its Maven coordinates.

The aggregator POM tells Maven which modules belong to the reactor build. A parent POM provides inherited configuration such as properties, dependency management and plugin management. One POM can serve both purposes, but aggregation and inheritance are separate concepts.

Maven's reactor determines the build order based on module relationships and dependencies. A module that depends on another module is normally built after its required project dependency.

Build all modules from the root:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

A targeted build can include a module and its required upstream projects:

```bash
mvn -pl service -am verify
```

Here, `-pl` selects the project list and `-am` also builds required projects in the reactor.

Multi-module structures help teams share versions and configuration, but excessive module coupling can make builds difficult to maintain. Define module boundaries around meaningful responsibilities and keep dependency direction understandable.

sections.title: Testing, Quality Gates and Build Verification
sections.content:
# Testing, Quality Gates and Build Verification

A Maven build should validate more than whether Java source code compiles. It should execute the appropriate tests and verification steps before an artifact is accepted for publication.

Unit tests are commonly executed by the Maven Surefire Plugin during the `test` phase. Integration tests can be managed with the Maven Failsafe Plugin, which separates integration-test execution from the final verification result.

A typical command is:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

This runs the lifecycle through `verify`, including earlier compilation and test phases and any additional verification goals bound to those phases.

A project may also integrate static analysis, code coverage, formatting checks, dependency analysis and vulnerability scanning. These tools are not automatically enabled simply because Maven is used; they must be configured as plugins or invoked by the CI pipeline.

Test reports are commonly generated under:

```text
target/surefire-reports/
target/failsafe-reports/
```

The actual report location can be changed through plugin configuration.

A reliable quality gate should define which failures block publication. Examples include failed tests, compilation errors, prohibited dependency versions, configured code-quality violations and security findings that exceed the team's accepted risk threshold.

Do not skip tests in a release pipeline merely to make a build pass. If a test is unstable, identify the cause, isolate external dependencies and correct the test or its environment.

The artifact should only move to publication after the required checks succeed. Preserve test reports and build logs so that failures can be investigated without repeating the entire build.

sections.title: Maven Packaging, Artifact Versioning and CI/CD Integration
sections.content:
# Maven Packaging, Artifact Versioning and CI/CD Integration

Maven packages application output into a distributable artifact. Common formats include JAR and WAR files. The selected packaging type and plugin configuration determine how the output is assembled.

For a JAR project:

```bash
mvn clean package
```

The artifact is commonly created under the `target` directory, with a name derived from the artifact ID and version.

For a Spring Boot application, the Spring Boot Maven Plugin can create an executable archive containing the application and its required runtime dependencies:

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
</plugin>
```

The plugin version should be managed consistently, often through the Spring Boot parent POM or dependency management conventions.

Artifact versioning should distinguish releases. Avoid publishing different binaries under the same immutable release coordinate. A CI build can derive a version from a release tag, build number or controlled versioning process.

A typical pipeline performs these steps:

1. Check out the required source revision.
2. Select the supported JDK and Maven environment.
3. Resolve dependencies from approved repositories.
4. Run `mvn clean verify`.
5. Publish test and verification reports.
6. Package and identify the artifact.
7. Publish the artifact to an artifact repository.
8. Pass the exact artifact version to deployment stages.

Build once and promote the same verified artifact across environments. Rebuilding separately for development, staging and production can produce different binaries if dependencies, plugins or build settings change.

Keep artifact coordinates, source commit, build identifier and checksum together so that a deployed release can be traced back to its source and build execution.

sections.title: Maven Build Troubleshooting and Production Engineering Lab
sections.content:
# Maven Build Troubleshooting and Production Engineering Lab

This lab investigates a Maven build that works on a developer laptop but fails on a clean CI agent.

Start by recording the environment:

```bash
java -version
mvn -version
```

Check that Maven is using the intended JDK. A common problem is that the shell, IDE and CI agent use different Java installations.

Inspect the project configuration:

```bash
mvn help:effective-pom
mvn help:active-profiles
```

Review inherited plugin settings, active profiles, dependency versions and compiler configuration.

If dependency resolution fails, inspect the dependency graph:

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
```

Verify repository URLs, credentials, proxy settings and access permissions. A dependency available in a developer's local `.m2` cache may not be available to a fresh CI agent.

For a controlled retry of remote snapshot or release metadata resolution, use Maven's update option:

```bash
mvn -U clean verify
```

Do not delete the entire local repository as the first troubleshooting step. Identify the failing artifact and determine whether the issue is a missing artifact, corrupted cache entry, repository outage or authorization failure.

For plugin failures, inspect the plugin version and effective configuration. For test failures, review Surefire or Failsafe reports and determine whether the failure is caused by application behavior, test data, environment configuration or an external service.

For packaging failures, verify the configured packaging type, plugin executions and generated files under `target`.

After correcting the issue, run the same build command on a clean environment. Confirm that compilation, tests, verification and packaging succeed and that the produced artifact has the expected coordinates and checksum.

In CI/CD, archive build logs and test reports, publish only verified artifacts, protect repository credentials and retain source revision metadata. This creates a traceable build process that can be repeated and audited.
