SpringApplication Startup and Application Bootstrap
Spring Boot Starter Dependencies and Dependency Management
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Starter Dependencies and Dependency Management

Spring Boot starters are dependency descriptors that bring together commonly required libraries for a particular application capability. They reduce the need to declare each supporting library individually.

For example, a web application can include the web starter:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

This starter brings in Spring MVC and the required web infrastructure, including a supported embedded servlet container through the dependency set selected by the Boot version.

A test starter provides common testing libraries:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

Other starters support data access, validation, security, messaging, monitoring and other capabilities. The exact libraries and versions depend on the selected Spring Boot release.

Spring Boot dependency management can be provided through the Spring Boot parent POM or by importing the Spring Boot dependency BOM. These approaches centralize compatible dependency versions.

A parent POM example:

```xml
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.4.0</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>
```

The selected version is an example and should be replaced with the version approved for the project.

Do not independently override Spring Framework, logging or embedded-server dependencies without checking compatibility. Uncontrolled version overrides can create linkage errors, startup failures and runtime incompatibilities.

Inspect resolved dependencies with:

```bash
mvn dependency:tree
```

Review starter contents when diagnosing unexpected transitive dependencies. Add only the capabilities the application actually requires, and keep the framework version aligned with the supported JDK and deployment environment.

sections.title: Auto-Configuration and Conditional Bean Registration
Spring IoC Container, Beans and Component Scanning
sections.content:
# Spring IoC Container, Beans and Component Scanning

The Spring Inversion of Control container creates and manages objects known as beans. Instead of constructing every dependency manually, application classes declare the dependencies they require and allow Spring to assemble them.

Common component annotations include:

- `@Component` for a general managed component.
- `@Service` for service-layer components.
- `@Repository` for persistence-layer components.
- `@Controller` for MVC controllers.
- `@RestController` for REST response controllers.

Example:

```java
@Service
public class DeploymentService {
    public String deploymentStatus() {
        return "Deployment ready";
    }
}
```

Spring discovers annotated classes through component scanning when they are inside configured scan packages.

`@SpringBootApplication` includes component scanning based on the package of the annotated application class. Therefore, placing the main application class in a suitable root package helps Spring discover the application's components.

A class outside the scan boundary may not become a bean. This can result in a missing-bean or unsatisfied-dependency error during startup.

Beans can also be declared explicitly through `@Bean` methods inside `@Configuration` classes. This approach is useful for creating objects from third-party libraries that cannot be annotated directly.

Spring beans have scopes. The default singleton scope means one bean instance per bean definition within a given application context, not one instance for the entire JVM.

Use clear component boundaries and avoid placing business logic in configuration classes. Keep infrastructure construction, application services and web request handling separated so the application remains testable and maintainable.

sections.title: Embedded Web Servers and Servlet Application Runtime
sections.content:
# Embedded Web Servers and Servlet Application Runtime

Spring Boot can package an application with an embedded web server. This allows the application to start its own HTTP server without requiring an administrator to deploy the application archive into a separately managed servlet container.

For a servlet-based web application, Spring Boot commonly uses an embedded Tomcat server through its web starter. Other supported server implementations can be selected through dependency and configuration choices.

A typical executable JAR can be started with:

```bash
java -jar target/application.jar
```

The application starts the embedded server and listens on the configured HTTP port. The default port for a typical servlet-based Spring Boot web application is 8080 unless it is changed by configuration.

The port can be changed in application properties:

```properties
server.port=9090
```

When an HTTP request arrives, the servlet container accepts the connection and passes the request through the servlet processing model. In Spring MVC, the `DispatcherServlet` acts as the front controller and routes requests to matching controller methods.

A port-binding failure can occur when another process already uses the configured port. A containerized service can also fail to receive traffic if it listens on an unexpected interface or port.

In Docker or Kubernetes, the application listening port, container port declaration, service target port and external routing configuration must agree.

Do not assume that declaring a container port automatically changes the Spring Boot server port. Configure the application and its deployment resources consistently.

For production use, configure connection limits, request timeouts, graceful shutdown behavior and resource capacity according to the server implementation and application workload.

sections.title: Externalized Configuration and Configuration Properties
sections.content:
# Externalized Configuration and Configuration Properties

Externalized configuration allows an application to use different settings without changing its compiled source code. This is important when the same artifact must run in development, testing and production environments.

Spring Boot supports configuration through property files, YAML files, environment variables, command-line arguments and other property sources.

Example:

```yaml
server:
  port: 8080

application:
  service-name: inventory-api
  request-timeout: 5s
```

Application configuration can be bound to a Java class using `@ConfigurationProperties`.

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "application")
public class ApplicationProperties {
    private String serviceName;
    private Duration requestTimeout;

    // getters and setters
}
```

Register the properties class through configuration properties scanning or explicit enablement.

Typed configuration is generally easier to validate and maintain than repeatedly reading raw property strings throughout business logic.

Use validation annotations when configuration values must satisfy constraints. For example, a timeout must be positive and a required endpoint must not be blank.

Environment variables are useful in container deployments because orchestration systems can supply environment-specific values at runtime.

Never store production passwords, API keys or private certificates in a source-controlled configuration file. Use an approved secret-management mechanism and restrict access to sensitive values.

A production configuration review should verify required properties, defaults, type conversions, validation, environment-specific overrides and secret handling. Missing critical settings should produce a clear startup failure rather than silently selecting an unsafe default.

sections.title: Spring Boot Profiles and Environment-Specific Behavior
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Profiles and Environment-Specific Behavior

Spring profiles provide a way to activate configuration and beans for particular environments or operating conditions. They help applications use different infrastructure settings while keeping the application code and build artifact consistent.

For example, a project may define:

```text
application.yml
application-dev.yml
application-test.yml
application-prod.yml
```

A profile-specific file contains configuration that applies when the corresponding profile is active.

```yaml
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod

server:
  port: 8080
```

A profile can be activated through an environment variable:

```bash
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

It can also be supplied as a command-line argument:

```bash
java -jar application.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

Profiles can control configuration and conditional bean registration through annotations such as `@Profile`.

Do not use profiles as a replacement for a secure secret-management system. A production profile committed to source control must not contain real passwords or credentials.

The active profile should be visible in startup diagnostics so operators can verify which environment configuration was loaded.

Be careful when multiple profiles are active simultaneously. Property precedence and profile-specific configuration rules determine which value is selected.

For Kubernetes deployments, profile activation can be supplied through environment variables or application arguments. Keep the profile selection aligned with the deployment environment and avoid building a different application binary for each environment merely to change configuration.

sections.title: Spring Boot Logging, Diagnostics and Startup Reports
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Logging, Diagnostics and Startup Reports

Logging provides visibility into application startup, runtime behavior, failures and external interactions. Spring Boot includes a logging integration and commonly uses Logback through its default logging starter configuration.

Application code should use a logging API rather than printing operational messages directly to standard output.

```java
private static final Logger log =
    LoggerFactory.getLogger(DeploymentService.class);

public void deploy(String serviceName) {
    log.info("Starting deployment for service {}", serviceName);
}
```

Parameterized logging avoids unnecessary string construction when the log level is disabled.

Log levels commonly include TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN and ERROR. Production services should use levels that provide useful operational evidence without generating excessive noise or exposing sensitive data.

Spring Boot logging can be configured through properties:

```properties
logging.level.root=INFO
logging.level.com.example=DEBUG
```

Use DEBUG selectively because detailed logs can increase volume and may expose implementation information.

When startup fails, inspect the earliest meaningful exception and its complete cause chain. A final `ApplicationContext` failure often reports that the context could not start, while the underlying cause may be a missing bean, invalid property, unavailable database or occupied port.

Spring Boot's debug mode can also produce an auto-configuration condition report:

```bash
java -jar application.jar --debug
```

For production diagnostics, correlate application logs with deployment timestamps, request identifiers, container events and infrastructure metrics.

Avoid logging passwords, authorization headers, access tokens, personal data or complete sensitive request payloads. Logging should support incident response without creating a security or privacy incident of its own.

sections.title: Spring Boot Testing Strategy and Application Context Tests
Spring Boot Executable JAR Packaging and Runtime Deployment
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Executable JAR Packaging and Runtime Deployment

Spring Boot applications can be packaged as executable JAR files. The Spring Boot Maven Plugin can repackage the regular Maven artifact so that it can be launched directly with a Java runtime.

A common build command is:

```bash
mvn clean package
```

The executable archive is commonly produced under the Maven `target` directory.

Run it with:

```bash
java -jar target/application.jar
```

The executable archive contains application classes and the runtime dependencies needed by the packaged application. Its launcher arrangement allows the application to start through the configured Boot loader.

The build should use a controlled JDK and framework version. Record the source revision and artifact coordinates so that the deployed binary can be traced to its build.

A Docker image can copy the executable archive into a runtime image:

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/application.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

This is a basic example. Production images should use approved base images, security updates, appropriate user permissions and resource limits.

The application port must match the container and deployment configuration. Environment-specific settings should be supplied at runtime rather than embedded as production secrets in the archive.

For Kubernetes deployments, readiness and liveness behavior should reflect the application's actual startup and health requirements. A process that has started is not necessarily ready to serve traffic.

Promote the same verified artifact through environments and retain its checksum, build metadata and deployment record. This improves release traceability and reduces environment-specific build differences.

sections.title: Spring Boot Actuator, Health Endpoints and Operational Visibility
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Actuator, Health Endpoints and Operational Visibility

Spring Boot Actuator provides production-oriented management and monitoring capabilities. It exposes application information through endpoints that can report health, metrics, environment details and other operational data depending on the enabled configuration.

Add the Actuator starter:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

A common health endpoint is:

```text
/actuator/health
```

The health endpoint can report application health and, when configured, health information for relevant dependencies such as databases or other integrations.

Endpoint exposure must be configured deliberately. Do not expose every management endpoint publicly by default.

For example:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics
```

This configuration exposes selected web endpoints. Authentication, network restrictions and appropriate health-detail visibility must still be considered.

Liveness and readiness are different operational concepts. Liveness indicates whether an application should be restarted, while readiness indicates whether it should receive traffic. A dependency failure should not automatically cause a restart loop unless the application is genuinely unable to recover.

In Kubernetes, health endpoints can be used by probes when configured with suitable paths and thresholds. Probe timing must allow for real application startup and dependency initialization.

Metrics can be exported to monitoring systems through suitable integrations. Monitor request latency, error rates, JVM memory, garbage collection, thread counts and dependency health.

Actuator endpoints provide diagnostic information, but they do not replace centralized logging, infrastructure monitoring, alerting or incident-response procedures.

sections.title: Spring Boot Security, Failure Handling and Production Reliability
Production Hands-on Lab: Build, Run, Monitor and Troubleshoot
sections.content:
# Production Hands-on Lab: Build, Run, Monitor and Troubleshoot

This lab follows a small Spring Boot service from source code to a running application and then investigates common operational failures.

Start by confirming the Java and Maven versions:

```bash
java -version
mvn -version
```

Build the project and execute its verification lifecycle:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Confirm that compilation and tests completed successfully. Inspect the generated artifact under `target`.

Start the application:

```bash
java -jar target/application.jar
```

Observe startup logs and confirm the active profile, configured port and successful application-context initialization.

Check the health endpoint when Actuator is installed and exposed:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
```

If the application does not start, investigate the earliest startup exception. Verify the JDK, missing dependencies, invalid properties, active profiles, bean creation and port availability.

If the application starts but requests fail, inspect controller mappings, validation, security rules, downstream connectivity and application logs.

If health checks fail in Kubernetes, compare the probe path and port with the actual application configuration. Check container events, startup duration, readiness conditions and termination behavior.

If memory usage increases, compare JVM heap metrics with total container memory. Inspect garbage collection logs and allocation behavior rather than assuming the heap is the only source of process memory.

Before a production release, verify:

1. The selected JDK and framework versions are supported together.
2. Maven tests and required quality checks pass.
3. The packaged artifact is identifiable and reproducible.
4. Production configuration and secrets are supplied securely.
5. Health endpoints are exposed with appropriate access controls.
6. Container ports and orchestration probes match application settings.
7. Logs and metrics are available to the operations team.
8. Shutdown and recovery behavior have been tested.

Record the source revision, artifact version, configuration reference and deployment result. This provides a traceable path from the Maven build to the running Spring Boot service.

sections.title: Application Package Organization and Root Package Design
sections.content:
# Application Package Organization and Root Package Design

A Spring Boot application's package structure determines how source code is grouped and how framework component scanning discovers application components. A clear package design helps developers understand responsibilities and reduces accidental dependencies between unrelated features.

A common starting structure is:

```text
inventory-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/example/inventory/
    ├── InventoryApplication.java
    ├── controller/
    ├── service/
    ├── repository/
    ├── entity/
    ├── dto/
    ├── config/
    └── exception/
```

The main application class should normally be placed in a root package above the packages containing controllers, services, repositories and configuration classes.

```java
package com.example.inventory;

@SpringBootApplication
public class InventoryApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(InventoryApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

Spring Boot's default component scanning begins from the package containing the application class and scans its descendant packages. Placing the main class in a narrow subpackage can prevent components in sibling packages from being discovered.

Package names should describe application responsibilities rather than temporary implementation details. Avoid putting every class into one large package or creating many packages that contain only one unrelated class.

For larger systems, feature-based packaging can be more maintainable than a single global controller-service-repository hierarchy. For example, inventory, deployment and reporting features can each own their relevant components.

Choose a structure that makes dependencies visible, supports testing and allows teams to evolve features without changing unrelated parts of the application.

sections.title: Layered Architecture and Responsibility Boundaries
sections.content:
# Layered Architecture and Responsibility Boundaries

Layered architecture separates application responsibilities so that HTTP handling, business rules and data persistence do not become mixed into one class.

A typical Spring Boot service uses these layers:

- Presentation layer: receives requests and creates HTTP responses.
- Application or service layer: coordinates use cases and business operations.
- Persistence layer: loads and stores application data.
- Domain layer: represents business concepts and rules.
- Configuration layer: defines infrastructure and framework configuration.

A request commonly follows this path:

```text
HTTP Client
    |
    v
Controller
    |
    v
Service
    |
    v
Repository
    |
    v
Database
```

The controller should translate HTTP input into application calls. It should not contain complex database queries or all the business logic.

The service layer coordinates the operation, applies business rules and manages transaction boundaries where appropriate.

The repository layer isolates persistence operations. It should not decide how HTTP errors are formatted or how a user interface displays data.

This separation makes it possible to test business rules without starting an HTTP server or connecting to a real database.

Layered architecture is a useful default, but it should not become a reason to create unnecessary classes. A simple operation does not require several empty abstraction layers.

The important design goal is clear ownership: each component should have one understandable responsibility, and dependencies should flow in a controlled direction.

sections.content:
# Production Architecture Review and Maintainability Lab

This lab reviews the structure of a small Spring Boot inventory service and checks whether its responsibilities are separated correctly.

Start with a package layout such as:

```text
com.example.inventory
├── InventoryApplication.java
├── controller
├── service
├── repository
├── entity
├── dto
├── config
└── exception
```

Trace a create-inventory request from the HTTP controller to the service and then to the repository. Confirm that the controller does not contain database queries and the repository does not create HTTP response objects.

Review constructor injection. A service should clearly declare the dependencies it needs rather than searching for them globally or creating infrastructure objects directly inside business methods.

Check whether entities are exposed directly from REST endpoints. If so, introduce request and response DTOs where a separate API contract is needed.

Inspect transaction boundaries. Multi-step database operations that must succeed or fail together should use a suitable transaction boundary, usually around the application service operation.

Review exception handling and request validation. Confirm that invalid requests produce understandable client errors, missing resources return appropriate status codes and unexpected failures do not reveal internal implementation details.

Run the tests:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Check that service tests run without starting unnecessary infrastructure, controller tests verify HTTP behavior and integration tests cover important cross-component interactions.

Finally, inspect external configuration, logging and security. Verify that secrets are not committed, external clients use appropriate timeouts, logs avoid sensitive values and the application can be monitored in its deployment environment.

A well-structured application should make the request flow easy to follow, isolate business rules from infrastructure, allow focused tests and support safe changes as the codebase grows.

sections.content:
# Bean Scopes, Singleton Behavior and Request Isolation

Bean scope determines how many instances Spring creates and the context in which those instances are used.

The default Spring bean scope is singleton. A singleton bean has one instance per bean definition within a Spring container, not necessarily one instance for an entire distributed system or JVM.

Prototype scope creates a new instance when the container is asked to resolve that bean.

Web applications can also use request and session scopes. Request scope associates an instance with an HTTP request, while session scope associates an instance with an HTTP session.

```java
@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
public class JobExecutionContext {
}
```

A singleton service should normally be stateless or use thread-safe shared components. Since many requests may use the same singleton concurrently, mutable request-specific fields can cause data leakage between users.

Do not store the current user's identity, request parameters or temporary transaction state in ordinary mutable singleton fields.

Injecting a shorter-lived scoped bean into a longer-lived singleton requires appropriate scope handling, such as a scoped proxy or an object provider. Otherwise, the shorter-lived object may be resolved only once and reused unexpectedly.

Prototype objects also require attention: Spring creates them, but the container does not perform the same complete destruction management used for singleton beans.

Choose scopes based on lifecycle and concurrency requirements. The default singleton scope is usually correct for stateless services, repositories and application configuration components.

Circular Dependencies and Dependency Graph Design
sections.content:
# Circular Dependencies and Dependency Graph Design

A circular dependency occurs when two or more components depend on one another in a cycle.

For example:

```text
OrderService -> PaymentService
PaymentService -> OrderService
```

Neither component can be constructed cleanly through ordinary constructor injection because each requires the other to exist first.

Spring commonly detects unresolvable constructor dependency cycles during application startup and reports a bean creation failure.

The best solution is usually to redesign the dependency graph rather than force the container to work around the cycle.

Possible improvements include extracting shared behavior into a third component, introducing an application-level coordinator or publishing an event when one operation should react to another.

For example, an order service can request payment processing and publish an order event after successful completion. A separate listener can react without creating a direct dependency back to the order service.

Avoid introducing `@Lazy` or setter injection solely to hide a circular dependency. Such changes may allow startup but leave the architecture tightly coupled and harder to reason about.

When diagnosing a cycle, follow the complete chain of bean creation reported in the startup exception. Identify the responsibilities that create the cycle and decide which dependency should be removed or replaced by a clearer boundary.

A directed dependency graph should generally move toward stable, lower-level responsibilities. Keeping dependencies acyclic makes components easier to construct, test and maintain.

Dependency Injection Failure Diagnosis and Production Troubleshooting
sections.content:
# Dependency Injection Failure Diagnosis and Production Troubleshooting

Dependency injection problems frequently appear during application startup as bean creation or dependency resolution errors.

Common failures include:

- `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`: no suitable bean definition was found.
- `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`: multiple candidates match and selection is ambiguous.
- `UnsatisfiedDependencyException`: a required dependency could not be resolved.
- `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`: bean creation encountered a circular or re-entrant dependency problem.
- `BeanCreationException`: a bean failed during creation or initialization.

Start diagnosis with the first meaningful cause in the complete exception chain. The final exception may describe a general bean creation failure while a nested cause identifies the actual missing class, property or dependency.

Check whether the component has a supported stereotype annotation or an explicit `@Bean` definition. Confirm that its package is included in component scanning.

If multiple implementations exist, inspect `@Primary`, `@Qualifier` and bean names. If a bean is conditional, inspect its profile, required classes and property conditions.

Useful commands include:

```bash
mvn test
mvn spring-boot:run
mvn clean verify
```

Spring Boot's condition evaluation report can help explain why conditional auto-configuration did or did not apply. It is commonly enabled with the `--debug` startup option.

For production, avoid enabling highly verbose diagnostic output indefinitely. Capture relevant startup logs, effective non-secret configuration and deployment metadata through approved operational processes.

Fix the underlying dependency graph or configuration instead of adding arbitrary annotations until the application starts.

REST Architectural Principles and HTTP-Based Resource Communication
sections.content:
# REST Architectural Principles and HTTP-Based Resource Communication

REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style for designing networked applications around resources and their representations. REST is not a Java library or a specific HTTP framework. It describes constraints and design principles that help services communicate through a uniform interface.

A resource is an identifiable concept such as a customer, deployment, order or inventory item. A REST API exposes resources through URLs and allows clients to interact with them using HTTP methods.

For example:

```http
GET /api/deployments/42
Accept: application/json
```

The server may return a JSON representation of deployment 42. The URL identifies the resource, while the response body describes its current representation.

Important REST architectural constraints include client-server separation, stateless communication, cacheability, a uniform interface and a layered system. Code-on-demand is an optional constraint.

Stateless communication means that each request contains the information needed to understand and process that request. The server should not depend on hidden conversational state from an earlier request to interpret the next request.

A REST-style API should use HTTP semantics consistently. It should not treat every operation as an arbitrary POST request with action names embedded in the URL.

In Spring Boot, Spring MVC provides annotations and infrastructure for implementing HTTP endpoints. Developers remain responsible for choosing meaningful resources, HTTP behavior, status codes and response contracts.

sections.title: Resource Modeling, URI Naming and API Endpoint Design
sections.content:
# Resource Modeling, URI Naming and API Endpoint Design

Good API design begins by identifying the resources clients need to access and the relationships between those resources.

Use nouns to identify resources rather than placing implementation actions in every URL.

A deployment API might expose:

```text
GET    /api/deployments
GET    /api/deployments/42
POST   /api/deployments
PUT    /api/deployments/42
PATCH  /api/deployments/42
DELETE /api/deployments/42
```

The collection URI `/api/deployments` identifies the deployment collection. The URI `/api/deployments/42` identifies one deployment.

Nested paths can represent meaningful relationships, such as `/api/deployments/42/events`, when events are resources associated with a deployment.

Avoid exposing Java class names, database table names or internal implementation details in public URLs. API resources should represent concepts that make sense to clients.

Use consistent pluralization, predictable identifier formats and a documented naming convention. Avoid unnecessary nesting because deeply nested URLs can make resource relationships difficult to manage.

A URI should identify a resource, while the HTTP method expresses the requested operation. For exceptional operations that do not map naturally to ordinary resource updates, model a meaningful subresource or explicit operation endpoint and document its behavior.

Resource modeling should also consider ownership and authorization. A syntactically valid resource identifier must not allow a caller to access another user's data.

In Spring Boot, use class-level `@RequestMapping` for a resource base path and method-level mappings for individual operations. Keep endpoint naming consistent across controllers.

sections.title: HTTP Methods, Safe Operations and Idempotency Semantics
sections.content:
# HTTP Methods, Safe Operations and Idempotency Semantics

HTTP methods communicate the intended operation on a resource. Correct method selection helps clients, proxies, caches and monitoring systems understand API behavior.

GET retrieves a representation and is defined as a safe method: it should not request a state-changing operation. HEAD is similar to GET but returns no response body. OPTIONS describes communication options supported by a resource.

POST commonly creates a subordinate resource or submits data for processing. PUT replaces the state of a resource at a known URI and is idempotent by HTTP semantics. PATCH applies a partial modification, with idempotency depending on the patch operation and its design. DELETE requests removal of a resource and is defined as idempotent.

Idempotency means that repeating the same request has the same intended effect as performing it once. For example, setting a deployment configuration to a particular value through PUT should not create additional deployments every time the request is repeated.

POST operations that create payments, orders or deployment jobs may be retried by clients after network failures. If duplicate execution would be harmful, design an idempotency mechanism such as a client-supplied idempotency key, persistent request tracking and safe result replay.

Do not assume that a request was not processed merely because the client did not receive a response. The server may have completed the operation before the connection failed.

In Spring MVC, map methods deliberately:

```java
@GetMapping("/{id}")
public DeploymentResponse find(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return deploymentService.find(id);
}
```

Document method semantics and retry behavior so clients can implement safe retries.

sections.title: HTTP Status Codes, Response Headers and Content Negotiation
sections.content:
# HTTP Status Codes, Response Headers and Content Negotiation

An HTTP response contains a status code, headers and, when appropriate, a response body. These elements communicate the outcome and metadata of an API operation.

Common status codes include:

- 200 OK: the request succeeded and a response representation is returned.
- 201 Created: a resource was created successfully.
- 202 Accepted: processing was accepted but may not have completed.
- 204 No Content: the request succeeded without a response body.
- 400 Bad Request: the request is invalid or cannot be processed as supplied.
- 401 Unauthorized: valid authentication credentials are required.
- 403 Forbidden: the caller is not permitted to perform the operation.
- 404 Not Found: the requested resource was not found or is intentionally concealed.
- 409 Conflict: the request conflicts with current resource state.
- 422 Unprocessable Content: the request is syntactically valid but its instructions cannot be processed.
- 500 Internal Server Error: an unexpected server failure occurred.
- 503 Service Unavailable: the service is temporarily unable to handle the request.

A create endpoint can return 201 Created and a Location header identifying the newly created resource.

Spring MVC provides `ResponseEntity` when a controller needs explicit control over status, headers and body:

```java
return ResponseEntity
    .created(URI.create("/api/deployments/42"))
    .body(response);
```

Content negotiation uses headers such as Accept to communicate which response media types a client can process. Content-Type describes the representation included in the request or response.

Use status codes consistently. Do not return 200 for every failure or expose internal exception messages as status descriptions.

Clients should be able to determine whether an operation succeeded, failed validation, conflicted with current state or requires authentication by examining the HTTP response.

JSON Serialization, Deserialization and API Data Contracts
sections.content:
# JSON Serialization, Deserialization and API Data Contracts

Serialization converts an application object into a representation such as JSON. Deserialization converts incoming JSON into a Java object.

Spring Boot commonly uses Jackson through Spring MVC HTTP message converters. A controller can return a response DTO and the framework serializes it according to the configured message converters and media type.

Example request:

```json
{
  "name": "production-deployment",
  "environment": "production"
}
```

A Java request model can represent the contract:

```java
public record CreateDeploymentRequest(
    String name,
    String environment
) {}
```

A response DTO should expose the fields clients are allowed and expected to receive. Avoid returning persistence entities directly because they may contain internal fields, lazy-loaded relationships or implementation details.

Serialization behavior can be affected by property names, null handling, date formats, enum representations and custom serializers. Changes to these settings can affect existing API consumers.

Do not expose secrets, internal tokens, password hashes or sensitive infrastructure metadata in JSON responses. Explicit response models make the public data contract easier to review.

For date and time values, choose a clear representation and timezone policy. ISO 8601 timestamps with an explicit offset or UTC indication are commonly suitable for interoperable APIs.

Deserialization should reject or safely handle malformed input. Unknown-field behavior should be chosen deliberately based on compatibility requirements.

Treat JSON as a versioned external contract. Test representative request and response payloads so accidental serialization changes are discovered before deployment.

Pagination, Filtering, Sorting and Collection Endpoint Design
sections.content:
# Pagination, Filtering, Sorting and Collection Endpoint Design

Collection endpoints can return large amounts of data. Pagination, filtering and sorting allow clients to retrieve manageable subsets instead of loading an entire dataset.

A page-based API might accept:

```http
GET /api/deployments?page=0&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc
```

Spring Data provides `Pageable`, `Page` and `Sort` abstractions that can be used by repository and service layers.

```java
@GetMapping
public Page<DeploymentResponse> list(Pageable pageable) {
    return deploymentService.list(pageable);
}
```

A `Page` includes content and metadata such as the total number of elements and pages. A `Slice` can be useful when the application needs to know whether another slice exists without requiring a total-count query.

Filtering can use explicit query parameters such as environment, status and creation date. Validate filter values and avoid constructing unsafe query fragments directly from user input.

Always enforce a maximum page size. Allowing an unbounded page request can produce expensive database queries, large memory allocations and slow responses.

For very large or frequently changing datasets, cursor-based pagination may provide more stable traversal than offset-based pagination. A cursor should represent a well-defined ordering position and should not be trusted as an authorization mechanism.

Sorting should use an allowlist of supported fields. Do not pass arbitrary client-supplied property names into dynamic query construction without validation.

Test pagination boundaries, empty results, invalid page sizes, sort direction and combined filters. Monitor query execution time and database indexes as collection volume grows.

sections.title: Idempotency Keys, Concurrency Control and Safe Retries
sections.content:
# Idempotency Keys, Concurrency Control and Safe Retries

Distributed clients and servers can experience timeouts, connection resets and retries. A client may not know whether a request completed before the connection failed.

For operations such as payment creation, order submission or deployment initiation, repeated requests must not accidentally create duplicate business effects.

An idempotency key is a client-generated identifier associated with one logical operation. The server stores the key, the operation state and, when appropriate, the result. A repeated request with the same key can return the previously recorded outcome instead of executing the operation again.

A reliable implementation should define key ownership, retention period, request fingerprint validation, concurrent request handling and behavior when the same key is reused with different content.

Idempotency is not a substitute for database transaction design. The operation record and business effect must be coordinated so that a crash cannot leave the system in an inconsistent state.

Concurrency control addresses competing updates to the same resource. Optimistic locking can use a version field or HTTP conditional requests such as ETag and If-Match.

If a client sends an update based on an outdated version, the server can reject it with an appropriate conflict or precondition status instead of silently overwriting newer data.

Retries should use bounded attempts, timeouts and backoff. Do not retry every failure blindly, especially when an operation may have a non-repeatable external side effect.

Document retry behavior and concurrency rules so API clients can interact safely during network failures and simultaneous updates.

sections.title: API Versioning, Backward Compatibility and Contract Evolution
sections.content:
# API Versioning, Backward Compatibility and Contract Evolution

An API contract changes as application requirements evolve. New fields, changed validation rules, renamed properties and different response structures can affect existing consumers.

Backward-compatible changes commonly include adding an optional response field or adding a new endpoint without changing existing behavior. Removing fields, changing their meaning, changing types or making previously optional input mandatory can break clients.

Versioning provides a way to introduce incompatible contract changes while giving consumers time to migrate.

Common approaches include URI versioning:

```text
/api/v1/deployments
/api/v2/deployments
```

Other approaches use custom request headers or media-type negotiation. Each approach has operational and documentation trade-offs.

Spring MVC can expose different mappings for versioned paths, while shared service logic can remain common when the underlying business behavior is unchanged.

Avoid creating a new version for every small change. Define which changes are compatible, how long old versions will be supported and how clients will be notified of deprecation.

Contract tests can help detect accidental breaking changes. Maintain representative examples and verify that existing clients continue to receive the fields and status behavior they depend on.

Versioning also requires an operational plan: monitor usage of older versions, publish migration guidance and remove deprecated endpoints only after the agreed support period.

The goal is controlled API evolution, not simply placing a version number in a URL while allowing incompatible behavior to change without notice.
