REST API Security, Authentication and Authorization Boundaries
sections.content:
# REST API Security, Authentication and Authorization Boundaries

REST endpoints are exposed to network clients and must enforce authentication, authorization and input controls at the server boundary.

Authentication establishes who or what is making a request. Authorization determines whether that authenticated principal is allowed to perform a particular operation on a particular resource.

Spring Security can protect HTTP endpoints using configured security filters and authentication mechanisms. Depending on the architecture, applications may use session-based authentication, OAuth 2.0 resource-server support with JWTs, opaque tokens or another approved mechanism.

A controller should not assume that a resource identifier proves ownership. A user who can request `/api/deployments/42` must still be checked against the authorization rules for deployment 42.

Apply authorization at appropriate request and method boundaries. Method-level security can protect business operations when enabled and configured deliberately.

Validate all external input. Use parameterized database operations and avoid unsafe string concatenation in queries. Configure CORS narrowly for the required browser origins rather than allowing every origin without a clear reason.

Protect sensitive data in transit with HTTPS. Do not place access tokens or passwords in URLs, because URLs can appear in logs, browser history and intermediary systems.

Rate limiting and abuse controls may be needed for exposed endpoints, particularly expensive operations and authentication-related routes.

Security tests should cover unauthenticated access, insufficient permissions, cross-user resource access, invalid tokens and unexpected request values. Never rely only on hiding an endpoint in the frontend.

sections.title: REST API Testing, Integration Verification and Contract Testing
Production REST API Operations, Observability and Hands-on Lab
sections.content:
# Production REST API Operations, Observability and Hands-on Lab

A production REST API must be observable, resilient and operationally predictable. Correct controller code alone does not guarantee reliable service behavior under real traffic.

Use structured logs and correlation identifiers to connect a client request with relevant server-side events. Avoid logging authorization headers, access tokens, passwords or unnecessary personal information.

Measure request count, response latency, error rate and saturation. Distributed tracing can help identify slow downstream calls across services. Spring Boot Actuator and compatible observability integrations can expose operational signals when configured securely.

Set appropriate timeouts for database operations and external HTTP clients. Bound request sizes, collection page sizes and expensive processing operations.

Use connection pools and database indexes according to measured workload. Monitor thread usage, connection-pool saturation and slow queries rather than assuming that a successful local test proves production performance.

A practical lab can implement a deployment API with these endpoints:

```text
POST   /api/deployments
GET    /api/deployments/{id}
GET    /api/deployments?page=0&size=20
PATCH  /api/deployments/{id}
DELETE /api/deployments/{id}
```

Create request and response DTOs, validate inputs, use a service for business rules and a repository for persistence. Return appropriate HTTP status codes and a consistent error representation.

Add authentication and resource-level authorization. Test missing resources, invalid input, duplicate submissions, stale updates and unauthorized requests.

Generate and review the OpenAPI specification. Run the test suite and build verification:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Before deployment, verify HTTPS configuration, secrets handling, logging redaction, timeout settings, health checks, database migration strategy and rollback readiness.

Finally, exercise the API under realistic request volume. Review latency percentiles, error rates and resource consumption. A production-ready API should have a documented contract, predictable failure behavior and enough operational visibility to diagnose incidents.

sections.title: Externalized Configuration and Spring Boot Property Sources
sections.content:
# Externalized Configuration and Spring Boot Property Sources

Externalized configuration allows an application to use settings supplied outside its compiled Java code. The same application artifact can therefore run in development, testing, staging and production with different database URLs, service endpoints, feature flags and operational settings.

Spring Boot reads configuration from several property sources. Depending on the application and startup method, these can include packaged configuration files, external configuration files, environment variables, Java system properties, command-line arguments and test-specific property sources.

For example, a database connection should not be hardcoded in a service:

```properties
spring.datasource.url=${DB_URL}
spring.datasource.username=${DB_USERNAME}
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}
```

The deployment environment supplies the actual values. The application reads them through Spring's Environment abstraction or binds them to typed configuration objects.

A property source is a source of key-value configuration. When multiple sources define the same key, Spring's property resolution rules determine which value is effective. The ordering matters because a command-line override may intentionally replace a packaged default.

Externalized configuration improves portability and deployment safety, but it does not automatically protect secrets. Passwords and tokens still need secure storage, access control and rotation.

A production application should define safe defaults where appropriate, explicitly require critical settings and document which deployment environment supplies each operational value.

sections.title: application.properties and application.yml Configuration Formats
sections.content:
# application.properties and application.yml Configuration Formats

Spring Boot supports both Java properties files and YAML configuration files. The conventional locations include `src/main/resources/application.properties` and `src/main/resources/application.yml`.

A properties file uses one key-value pair per line:

```properties
server.port=8081
spring.application.name=inventory-service
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
```

YAML expresses hierarchical configuration through indentation:

```yaml
server:
  port: 8081

spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info
```

Both formats can represent nested configuration. The YAML hierarchy is often easier to read for deeply nested settings, while properties files make individual key-value settings explicit.

YAML indentation is significant. Tabs, inconsistent spaces and incorrect nesting can cause parsing errors or place a setting under the wrong parent. Use spaces consistently and validate YAML before deployment.

Do not maintain conflicting copies of the same settings in both formats without a clear reason. If both files define a property, the effective value depends on Spring Boot's configuration loading and property-source precedence rules.

Use descriptive keys that follow the framework's documented naming conventions. For application-owned settings, group related properties under a stable prefix such as `inventory`, `notifications` or `deployment`.

Choose one primary format for each configuration layer and keep it readable, reviewable and version-controlled. Configuration changes should receive the same review discipline as application code.

sections.title: Property Precedence, Overrides and Configuration Resolution
sections.content:
# Property Precedence, Overrides and Configuration Resolution

A Spring Boot application may receive the same property from several sources. Property precedence determines which value wins when duplicate keys are present.

For example, a packaged default might define:

```properties
server.port=8080
```

A deployment environment may override it:

```text
SERVER_PORT=9090
```

A command-line argument can also supply an override:

```bash
java -jar inventory-service.jar --server.port=9080
```

Spring Boot uses an ordered set of property sources. Higher-precedence sources override lower-precedence sources for the same property. Command-line arguments and test-specific sources are examples of sources that can override ordinary configuration-file values.

The exact order can depend on the Spring Boot version, configuration mechanism and application startup context. Consult the version-matched external configuration reference instead of relying on assumptions about every source.

Property resolution also supports placeholders:

```properties
app.storage.location=${STORAGE_LOCATION:/var/lib/inventory}
```

The placeholder uses `STORAGE_LOCATION` when available and otherwise applies the specified default.

A missing required placeholder without a default can prevent startup. This is useful for critical configuration because the application fails early rather than running with an invalid endpoint or empty credential.

When diagnosing an unexpected value, inspect all possible sources: packaged files, external files, environment variables, JVM properties, command-line arguments, active profiles and test overrides.

Never print complete environment dumps into public logs because they may contain credentials or other sensitive values.

sections.title: Environment Variables, JVM Properties and Command-Line Overrides
sections.content:
# Environment Variables, JVM Properties and Command-Line Overrides

Deployment systems frequently supply configuration through environment variables, Java system properties and command-line arguments. These mechanisms allow operators to change runtime settings without rebuilding the application.

Spring Boot supports relaxed binding for environment variables. A property such as:

```properties
spring.datasource.url
```

can commonly be supplied using an environment variable such as:

```text
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL
```

A JVM system property can be supplied using the Java `-D` option:

```bash
java -Dserver.port=9090 -jar inventory-service.jar
```

A Spring Boot command-line property can be passed as an application argument:

```bash
java -jar inventory-service.jar --server.port=9091
```

These are different mechanisms: `-D` sets a Java system property, while `--server.port` is an application command-line property interpreted by Spring Boot.

In Docker, environment variables can be provided through the container runtime:

```bash
docker run -e SERVER_PORT=9090 inventory-service:1.0
```

In Kubernetes, values can be supplied through a Deployment's environment configuration and referenced from ConfigMaps or Secrets.

Avoid embedding passwords and tokens in shell command histories or process arguments. Use approved secret injection mechanisms and restrict access to deployment definitions.

Document which configuration source is authoritative for each environment. Multiple uncontrolled overrides make production behavior difficult to reproduce and troubleshoot.

sections.title: Type-Safe Configuration with ConfigurationProperties
sections.content:
# Type-Safe Configuration with ConfigurationProperties

Reading every property individually using `@Value` can become difficult when an application has many related settings. Spring Boot provides `@ConfigurationProperties` to bind a group of properties into a structured Java object.

For example:

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "inventory")
public record InventoryProperties(
    String region,
    int maximumItems,
    Duration refreshInterval
) {}
```

Configuration can be supplied through YAML:

```yaml
inventory:
  region: ap-south
  maximum-items: 500
  refresh-interval: 30s
```

The configuration object groups related values under a meaningful prefix. Supported conversion allows values such as duration strings to be represented as Java types.

Register configuration properties using `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` or `@EnableConfigurationProperties` as appropriate for the application.

A configuration properties class provides a central place to understand which settings a feature requires. It also supports metadata generation for IDE assistance when the appropriate configuration processor is configured.

Prefer suitable types instead of representing every setting as a String. Use `Duration` for time intervals, `DataSize` for sizes and enums for a fixed set of supported choices.

Do not place business operations inside configuration classes. Their responsibility is to represent and expose validated configuration values.

For a large application, group properties by feature or infrastructure responsibility. This improves discoverability and makes configuration changes easier to review.

sections.title: Configuration Validation, Defaults and Fail-Fast Startup
Custom Application Properties and Feature-Specific Configuration
sections.content:
# Custom Application Properties and Feature-Specific Configuration

Spring Boot applications often require settings that do not belong to built-in framework properties. Examples include retry limits, notification endpoints, feature toggles, retention periods and business-specific thresholds.

Use a consistent application-owned prefix:

```yaml
deployment:
  notifications:
    enabled: true
    endpoint: https://notifications.internal
  retry:
    maximum-attempts: 3
    initial-delay: 2s
```

Bind these values into a dedicated configuration properties type rather than scattering property strings throughout controllers and services.

For example:

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "deployment.retry")
public record RetryProperties(
    int maximumAttempts,
    Duration initialDelay
) {}
```

A service can receive the properties through constructor injection and use them when coordinating retry behavior.

Avoid using generic names such as `enabled`, `timeout` or `url` at the application root. Feature-specific prefixes make settings easier to locate and reduce naming collisions.

Separate configuration that describes infrastructure from configuration that represents business policy. A database URL is infrastructure configuration, while a deployment retry policy may be an application behavior setting.

Do not confuse configuration with mutable runtime state. A property is normally an input used to configure the application; changing a file does not automatically guarantee that every already-created bean will update its behavior.

For dynamic configuration, define an explicit refresh or reload architecture with validation, consistency rules and operational controls. Otherwise, prefer immutable configuration established during startup.

sections.title: Secrets Management, Credential Injection and Sensitive Configuration
sections.content:
# Secrets Management, Credential Injection and Sensitive Configuration

Configuration frequently includes sensitive values such as database passwords, API tokens, signing keys and external-service credentials. These values require stronger protection than ordinary application settings.

Do not commit production secrets to Git repositories, Docker images, packaged JAR files or public configuration examples.

For local development, use an approved local secret mechanism or environment-specific credentials that are not committed. For production, use an organizational secret manager or platform-supported secret injection mechanism.

In Kubernetes, a Secret can be referenced by a container environment variable or mounted as a file. Kubernetes Secret data is not automatically safe merely because it uses the Secret resource type; access control, encryption at rest, cluster security and delivery practices must also be configured.

A deployment may reference a secret-backed environment variable:

```yaml
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: inventory-db-credentials
        key: password
```

The Spring Boot configuration can then reference `DB_PASSWORD` through a placeholder.

Restrict who can read, modify and deploy secrets. Apply least privilege and separate credentials between development, staging and production.

Rotate credentials according to the organization's policy and design applications to handle rotation safely. Avoid printing secret values in startup logs, exception messages, diagnostics or monitoring labels.

Configuration review should distinguish ordinary operational settings from secrets and verify that each sensitive value has an approved source, access policy and rotation process.

sections.title: Config Imports, External Configuration Files and Config Trees
sections.content:
# Config Imports, External Configuration Files and Config Trees

Spring Boot supports configuration loading from locations outside the packaged application. This allows operators to provide deployment-specific settings without modifying the application artifact.

External configuration can be supplied through supported filesystem locations, additional locations and imports. For example, an application can import another configuration resource:

```properties
spring.config.import=optional:file:./config/extra.properties
```

The `optional:` prefix indicates that the resource may be absent without causing the import itself to fail. Do not mark a critical production configuration resource optional if the application cannot operate safely without it.

`spring.config.location` and `spring.config.additional-location` serve different purposes. A location setting can change where configuration is loaded from, while an additional location supplements the normal search locations. Their replacement and precedence behavior should be checked against the Spring Boot version in use.

Config trees allow files in a directory to be mapped into configuration properties. This is useful when platform secret systems mount individual values as files rather than exposing them as environment variables.

For example, a mounted directory can contain a file named `db.password`, whose contents become the value of the corresponding property when a suitable config-tree import is configured.

Protect filesystem permissions and ensure mounted configuration is available before the application starts.

Test external configuration loading in the same way it will be used in deployment. A file path that works on a developer laptop may not exist inside a container or Kubernetes pod.

sections.title: Configuration Binding Diagnostics and Actuator Environment Inspection
sections.content:
# Configuration Binding Diagnostics and Actuator Environment Inspection

Configuration problems can be difficult to diagnose because the application may receive values from several sources. The first task is to identify the effective property value and the source that supplied it.

Spring Boot Actuator provides operational endpoints that can help inspect application configuration when enabled and appropriately secured.

The `env` endpoint exposes environment properties and property-source information. The `configprops` endpoint provides information about configuration properties beans and their bound values.

These endpoints can reveal whether a property is missing, overridden or bound differently from what the deployment expected.

Actuator endpoint exposure must be configured deliberately. Do not expose environment or configuration-property diagnostics publicly because they may reveal internal endpoints, usernames, infrastructure details or sensitive configuration metadata.

For example, expose only the health endpoint over an externally accessible management interface unless other endpoints have a clear operational need:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health
```

For authorized internal troubleshooting, additional endpoints may be enabled behind appropriate authentication and network controls.

The `--debug` startup option can help explain Spring Boot auto-configuration decisions, but it is not a replacement for inspecting property-source precedence or validating bound configuration.

When a property is incorrect, check its spelling, prefix, active profile, source file location, environment variable name, placeholder and override order.

Use redacted diagnostic output. Never copy raw secret-bearing endpoint responses into tickets, terminal logs or public incident reports.

sections.title: Configuration Testing and Environment-Specific Verification
sections.content:
# Configuration Testing and Environment-Specific Verification

Configuration is part of application behavior and should be tested. A service that passes unit tests with developer defaults may still fail when deployed with production configuration.

Unit tests can construct configuration properties directly and verify behavior for different values. Spring Boot tests can also load property sources and validate binding.

For example, a test can supply an explicit property:

```java
@SpringBootTest(properties = {
    "inventory.region=ap-south",
    "inventory.maximum-items=200"
})
class InventoryConfigurationTest {
}
```

Use focused tests to verify required properties, defaults, type conversion and validation constraints. A missing mandatory endpoint should fail clearly rather than allowing the application to start in a partially configured state.

Test profile-specific configuration with the appropriate active profile. Confirm that a development profile cannot accidentally select fake infrastructure in production.

For external configuration files, test the actual file format and loading mechanism. For environment variables, verify the deployment naming convention and the final bound property value without exposing sensitive content.

CI/CD pipelines can run configuration validation for each deployment target. This can catch missing variables, invalid durations, unsupported feature combinations and incorrect service endpoints before rollout.

Do not copy production secrets into test fixtures. Use test credentials, mocks or controlled test services.

A reliable configuration test suite verifies both positive cases and failure cases. It should prove that valid configuration works and invalid or incomplete configuration is rejected predictably.

sections.title: Production Configuration Governance and Hands-on Deployment Lab
sections.content:
# Production Configuration Governance and Hands-on Deployment Lab

Production configuration must be reproducible, secure and consistent with the version of the application being deployed.

Build an inventory service with a typed configuration prefix:

```yaml
inventory:
  region: ap-south
  maximum-items: 500
  refresh-interval: 30s

spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service
```

Create an `InventoryProperties` type using `@ConfigurationProperties`. Register it through configuration-property scanning or explicit enablement and validate critical fields.

Supply the database URL and credentials through deployment-managed values rather than committing them into the repository.

For local execution, use an approved local configuration source. For Docker, inject environment variables through the container runtime or orchestrator. For Kubernetes, reference ConfigMaps for ordinary settings and Secrets for sensitive values.

Verify the application using:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Run the packaged application with an explicit override:

```bash
java -jar target/inventory-service.jar --server.port=9090
```

Confirm that the intended port is effective. Verify the active profile and inspect configuration binding through safe diagnostics.

Create a deployment checklist that covers required properties, defaults, precedence, secret sources, file mounts, timeouts, external endpoints and profile selection.

Before rollout, compare the configuration contract with the application version. A deployment should not silently depend on a property that has not been introduced or supported by that version.

For production governance, review changes, restrict secret access, record configuration ownership and establish rollback procedures. Monitor startup failures and configuration-related incidents.

The final objective is to deploy the same tested artifact across environments while changing only the approved external configuration, without exposing credentials or relying on undocumented machine-specific settings.

sections.title: Spring Profiles and Environment-Specific Application Behavior
sections.content:
# Spring Profiles and Environment-Specific Application Behavior

Spring Profiles provide a mechanism for activating environment-specific configuration and bean definitions. They allow one application codebase to behave differently in development, testing, staging and production without maintaining separate application builds.

A profile can control which configuration classes and beans are active. For example, a development environment may use a local service implementation, while production uses an integration with a real external system.

A profile is activated through supported configuration mechanisms such as an environment variable, JVM system property or command-line argument:

```bash
java -jar inventory-service.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev
```

A profile can also be activated through an environment variable:

```text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev
```

A class or configuration method can be restricted to a profile:

```java
@Component
@Profile("dev")
public class DevelopmentNotificationSender {
}
```

Profiles should represent meaningful deployment configurations rather than every small feature choice. Too many overlapping profiles can make application behavior difficult to understand.

A profile does not automatically create a separate database, network or security boundary. It only controls configuration and bean selection within the application. The infrastructure and permissions must still be configured independently.

Use profiles to select environment-specific behavior deliberately, while keeping common business logic consistent across environments.

sections.title: Profile-Specific Configuration Files and Property Loading
sections.content:
# Profile-Specific Configuration Files and Property Loading

Spring Boot supports profile-specific configuration files. A common convention is to maintain a shared `application.yml` file and separate files for individual environments.

For example:

```text
src/main/resources/
├── application.yml
├── application-dev.yml
├── application-test.yml
└── application-prod.yml
```

The shared file contains common settings:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service

server:
  port: 8080
```

The development file can define environment-specific values:

```yaml
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: dev

inventory:
  endpoint: http://localhost:9090
```

The production file can contain production-specific non-secret settings:

```yaml
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod

inventory:
  endpoint: https://inventory.internal
```

When the matching profile is active, Spring Boot includes the corresponding profile-specific configuration. The effective property value depends on the configuration loading rules and property-source precedence.

Do not copy every common property into every profile file. Duplicating configuration increases maintenance work and can cause environments to drift unexpectedly.

Keep secrets out of packaged profile files. Supply sensitive values through an approved secret-management mechanism.

Profile-specific files are part of the application configuration contract. Validate that the correct files are included in the build and that each deployment activates the intended profile.

sections.title: Activating Profiles Through CLI, JVM and Environment Variables
sections.content:
# Activating Profiles Through CLI, JVM and Environment Variables

Spring profiles can be activated through several runtime configuration mechanisms. This makes it possible for the same executable JAR to run with different profile selections in different deployment environments.

Using a Spring Boot command-line argument:

```bash
java -jar inventory-service.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod
```

Using a Java system property:

```bash
java -Dspring.profiles.active=prod -jar inventory-service.jar
```

Using an environment variable:

```text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

The command-line argument and JVM property are different inputs. The first is an application argument interpreted by Spring Boot, while the second is a Java system property.

For Docker, the active profile can be passed through the container environment:

```bash
docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod inventory-service:1.0
```

For Kubernetes, the environment variable can be declared in the container specification and supplied through an approved deployment configuration.

Do not activate a production profile by hardcoding it into the application source. The deployment environment should explicitly determine the intended runtime configuration.

Check the effective active profiles during startup and make them visible through safe operational diagnostics. Avoid logging secrets or dumping every environment variable.

When multiple configuration mechanisms specify profile activation, investigate the effective configuration rather than assuming that the last setting in a deployment script always wins.

sections.title: Default Profiles, Profile Groups and Composite Environments
sections.content:
# Default Profiles, Profile Groups and Composite Environments

Spring supports default profiles that are used when no active profile has been selected. The default profile name is `default` unless the application changes it.

A default profile can provide safe baseline configuration:

```yaml
spring:
  profiles:
    default: local
```

Default profiles are not the same as explicitly active profiles. A default is used when no active profile has been selected, while active profiles determine which profile-specific configuration and beans are enabled.

Spring Boot also supports profile groups. A group allows one logical profile to activate a set of related profiles.

```yaml
spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      production:
        - prod-database
        - prod-observability
        - prod-integrations
```

Activating `production` activates the profiles included in the group. This can simplify deployments where several coordinated configuration areas must be enabled together.

Profile groups are useful when a deployment environment has several independent configuration concerns, but they should not be used to create a confusing collection of overlapping settings.

Keep profile names meaningful and document the purpose of each group. Avoid naming a profile after a temporary developer machine or a single person's local workflow.

Do not assume that every combination of profiles is valid. Define supported combinations and test them explicitly.

A useful profile design has a clear default, a small number of deployment-oriented profiles and groups only where they improve operational clarity.

sections.title: Profile Precedence, Property Overrides and Configuration Conflicts
sections.content:
# Profile Precedence, Property Overrides and Configuration Conflicts

An application can load common properties, profile-specific files, external configuration and runtime overrides at the same time. Understanding the resulting property value is essential when diagnosing environment-specific behavior.

For example, the common configuration may define:

```yaml
inventory:
  endpoint: http://localhost:9090
```

A production profile may override it:

```yaml
inventory:
  endpoint: https://inventory.internal
```

A deployment environment can also provide a higher-precedence override through an environment variable or command-line property.

The effective value depends on Spring Boot's ordered property sources, configuration loading rules and active profiles. Profile-specific configuration does not mean that it always wins over every external source.

Multiple active profiles may contribute configuration. When the same key appears in several sources, the documented ordering rules determine the selected value.

Avoid defining the same critical property in many places. Multiple overrides make incidents difficult to diagnose because the value visible in one file may not be the value actually used at runtime.

Use a configuration ownership convention: common defaults belong in shared configuration, environment-specific non-secret settings belong in the appropriate environment source, and sensitive values belong in a secret-management system.

When a service connects to the wrong database or endpoint, verify active profiles, loaded configuration files, environment variables, JVM properties and command-line arguments.

Use protected diagnostics to identify the source of a property without exposing sensitive values.

sections.title: Profile-Based Bean Selection and Environment-Specific Integrations
Environment Variables and External Configuration in Deployment Pipelines
sections.content:
# Environment Variables and External Configuration in Deployment Pipelines

A deployment pipeline should build an application artifact once and promote that same artifact through development, testing, staging and production. Environment-specific configuration should be supplied at deployment or runtime rather than compiled into separate artifacts.

A pipeline can select the profile and inject non-secret configuration:

```yaml
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    value: prod
  - name: INVENTORY_ENDPOINT
    value: https://inventory.internal
```

The application can bind these values through Spring's configuration mechanisms.

Build-time configuration and runtime configuration serve different purposes. Build-time settings influence compilation or packaging, while runtime settings determine how the deployed process behaves.

Avoid creating a separate JAR for each environment merely to change a database URL or service endpoint. This increases the risk of deploying different code to different environments.

In Jenkins or another CI/CD system, keep environment-specific deployment parameters in controlled pipeline configuration. Protect credentials through the platform's credential-management feature rather than storing them in source files or shell scripts.

A promotion process should record the artifact version, target environment, selected profile and configuration revision. This makes it possible to reconstruct which application and configuration were running during an incident.

Validate mandatory configuration before traffic is routed to a new deployment. A missing endpoint or invalid profile selection should cause a clear deployment failure instead of silently creating an unhealthy service.

sections.title: Docker Runtime Profiles and Container Configuration
sections.content:
# Docker Runtime Profiles and Container Configuration

Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into a container image. Environment-specific configuration should generally be supplied when the container is started, not embedded as environment-specific values in the image.

A Spring Boot container can use an environment variable to select a profile:

```bash
docker run \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e INVENTORY_ENDPOINT=https://inventory.internal \
  inventory-service:1.0
```

The same image can be used in multiple environments by supplying different runtime configuration.

A Dockerfile should focus on building or running the application consistently. It should not contain production credentials or assume that every deployment uses the same endpoint.

A Compose file can define development-specific settings:

```yaml
services:
  inventory:
    image: inventory-service:1.0
    environment:
      SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: dev
      INVENTORY_ENDPOINT: http://inventory-mock:8080
```

This is useful for local integration testing, but production secrets should be managed through the deployment platform's secure mechanisms.

Container environment variables can be inspected by users with sufficient access to the Docker host or container runtime. Do not assume that putting a password in an environment variable makes it secret from privileged operators.

Verify that the container receives the expected profile, configuration files and network endpoints. Also confirm that the application listens on the expected interface and port inside the container.

A healthy container process does not necessarily mean that its selected profile or external configuration is correct. Use application health checks and runtime diagnostics to verify readiness.

sections.title: Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Secrets and Profile Injection
sections.content:
# Kubernetes ConfigMaps, Secrets and Profile Injection

Kubernetes provides ConfigMaps and Secrets for supplying configuration to containerized applications. A ConfigMap is intended for non-confidential configuration, while a Secret is intended for sensitive values.

A Deployment can activate a Spring profile through an environment variable:

```yaml
env:
  - name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
    value: prod
```

Ordinary configuration can be supplied from a ConfigMap:

```yaml
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: inventory-config
```

A sensitive value can be referenced from a Secret:

```yaml
env:
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: inventory-db
        key: password
```

Spring Boot can read these values through its normal property resolution mechanisms.

A ConfigMap or Secret can also be mounted as files. Spring Boot supports configuration imports, including config-tree imports, for directory-based configuration sources.

Kubernetes Secret objects require appropriate cluster security. Configure RBAC, encryption at rest where supported, controlled access and safe secret rotation. Base64 encoding is not encryption.

A configuration update does not guarantee that an already-running application automatically reloads every property. Environment variables are established for a container process at startup, and mounted file updates do not automatically refresh arbitrary Spring beans.

Use a controlled rollout or an explicitly designed refresh mechanism when configuration changes must take effect. Verify the active profile, mounted resources and effective settings after deployment without printing secret values.

sections.title: Profile Testing, Integration Tests and Environment Parity
sections.content:
# Profile Testing, Integration Tests and Environment Parity

Profiles change configuration and bean selection, so they should be tested as part of the application lifecycle.

Spring tests can activate a specific profile using `@ActiveProfiles`:

```java
@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("test")
class InventoryApplicationTest {
}
```

The test context loads the configuration associated with the selected profile and can verify that the expected beans are available.

Use focused tests for profile-specific components. For example, verify that the test profile selects a test database configuration and that the production profile does not accidentally register a fake payment gateway.

Integration tests should verify interactions with the infrastructure expected in the target environment. Use controlled test databases, containers or service doubles rather than connecting to production resources.

Environment parity means that environments should be similar enough for testing to reveal deployment problems. They do not need identical credentials or infrastructure sizes, but their application configuration, service interfaces and deployment behavior should be deliberately aligned.

Test configuration combinations that are officially supported. If production uses a profile group, verify that activating the group loads all required configuration and beans.

Include negative tests for missing mandatory properties, incompatible profiles and invalid configuration values.

Avoid relying on a developer's machine environment. Tests should declare their required profiles and configuration explicitly so that CI produces reproducible results.

sections.title: Profile Troubleshooting, Startup Diagnostics and Configuration Recovery
sections.content:
# Profile Troubleshooting, Startup Diagnostics and Configuration Recovery

A wrong active profile can cause an application to connect to the wrong service, select a fake implementation or load incomplete configuration. Profile-related failures should be diagnosed systematically.

Start by confirming the active profiles shown in safe startup logs or authorized operational diagnostics. Check the value of `spring.profiles.active` and determine whether it came from a command-line argument, JVM property, environment variable or configuration file.

Verify that the expected profile-specific file is packaged or mounted in the correct location. Check spelling, naming conventions and file syntax.

If a bean is missing, inspect its `@Profile` condition and confirm that the expected profile is active. If dependency resolution is ambiguous, determine whether multiple profile-specific implementations were registered together.

If a property has the wrong value, inspect all relevant property sources and precedence. Do not assume that editing `application-prod.yml` changes the value when a deployment environment variable overrides it.

Useful operational checks include:

```bash
printenv SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE
```

and reviewing the application's sanitized startup logs and deployment configuration.

For Docker, inspect the container's configured environment and mounted files using authorized runtime access. For Kubernetes, inspect the Deployment, ConfigMap references, Secret references and pod rollout state.

Never dump secret values into incident tickets or shared terminal output. Redact sensitive data before collecting diagnostics.

After correcting configuration, restart or roll out the application when required, verify readiness and confirm that the intended profile-specific integration is active.

sections.title: Production Environment Promotion and Hands-on Deployment Lab
sections.content:
# Production Environment Promotion and Hands-on Deployment Lab

This lab demonstrates how one Spring Boot artifact can be promoted across environments using different runtime profiles and external configuration.

Create a shared configuration file:

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: inventory-service

server:
  port: 8080
```

Create environment-specific files for development, testing and production. Keep common settings in the shared file and define only genuine differences in the environment-specific sources.

Implement a small service that receives an external endpoint through `@ConfigurationProperties`. Register a development implementation and a production implementation using explicit profiles.

Build the application once:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

Package the executable JAR and record its artifact version or checksum. Promote the same artifact through the deployment pipeline.

Run the development environment:

```bash
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev java -jar target/inventory-service.jar
```

Run the production configuration:

```bash
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar target/inventory-service.jar
```

Supply production credentials through an approved secret-management mechanism rather than adding them to the command line or repository.

For container deployment, pass the profile and ordinary configuration through controlled runtime settings. For Kubernetes, use a Deployment with ConfigMaps and Secrets and verify the resulting pod configuration.

Before production rollout, confirm that the intended profile is active, mandatory properties are present, the correct integration beans are selected and health checks succeed.

Record the artifact version, deployment environment, configuration revision and rollout outcome. Define rollback behavior if the new configuration prevents the application from becoming ready.

The lab is complete when the same tested artifact runs successfully in each supported environment, uses the intended external settings and does not expose credentials or rely on undocumented machine-specific configuration.

sections.title: Application Logging Architecture and the Role of Operational Logs
sections.content:
# Application Logging Architecture and the Role of Operational Logs

Application logging records important events that occur while a service is running. Logs help developers and operations engineers understand application behavior, investigate failures, identify security events and reconstruct the sequence of actions that led to an incident.

In a Spring Boot application, application code normally writes log events through a logging API such as SLF4J. A logging implementation such as Logback processes those events and sends them to configured destinations. Destinations may include the console, a file or an external log collection agent.

The application should log meaningful operational events rather than every internal variable. Examples include application startup, successful external service connections, failed requests, authentication failures and important business operation outcomes.

A useful logging architecture separates event creation from event storage and analysis. The application produces events, the runtime or logging framework writes them, and an agent or platform can collect and forward them to a centralized logging system.

Logs are not a replacement for metrics or distributed traces. Logs explain individual events, metrics summarize system behavior over time, and traces show request execution across services.

Define a logging policy that covers event meaning, severity, sensitive data handling, retention and access control. Production logging should provide enough evidence to investigate incidents without generating excessive noise or exposing confidential information.

sections.title: SLF4J, Logback and Spring Boot Logging Integration
Log Levels, Severity Classification and Logger Categories
sections.content:
# Log Levels, Severity Classification and Logger Categories

Log levels classify events according to their importance and operational meaning. Spring Boot applications commonly use TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN and ERROR.

TRACE is intended for highly detailed diagnostic information. DEBUG provides information useful during development and troubleshooting. INFO records normal application milestones. WARN identifies unexpected conditions that do not necessarily stop the application. ERROR indicates a failure that requires attention.

Example:

```java
log.debug("Loading inventory record: {}", itemId);
log.info("Inventory service started");
log.warn("Retrying unavailable supplier endpoint");
log.error("Inventory update failed for itemId={}", itemId, exception);
```

A logger's configured threshold controls which events are emitted. If the threshold is INFO, DEBUG and TRACE events are normally excluded.

Configure levels by package or class instead of enabling DEBUG globally across a large production service. For example:

```yaml
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example.inventory: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: WARN
```

Use ERROR for actual failures, not for every unsuccessful validation or expected business outcome. Use WARN for actionable conditions and avoid repeatedly logging the same harmless event at high severity.

Consistent severity classification makes log filtering and alert design more useful. A monitoring system that treats every warning as a critical incident will create alert fatigue.

Define clear rules for each level and ensure developers apply them consistently across application modules.

sections.title: Structured Logging, JSON Events and Machine-Readable Fields
sections.content:
# Structured Logging, JSON Events and Machine-Readable Fields

Structured logging records events as named fields rather than relying entirely on free-form text. This makes logs easier to search, filter, aggregate and analyze in centralized logging platforms.

A traditional message might say:

```text
Order processing failed for order 78421
```

A structured event can represent the same information using fields such as timestamp, level, service, event name and order identifier.

Example conceptual JSON event:

```json
{
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "order-service",
  "event": "order_processing_failed",
  "orderId": "78421",
  "message": "Order processing failed"
}
```

Structured output can be configured using an appropriate Logback encoder or logging integration. The exact configuration depends on the encoder dependency and its supported version.

Use stable field names across services. Common fields include service name, environment, timestamp, severity, trace identifier and event name.

Do not place sensitive information into structured fields simply because the output is machine-readable. Passwords, access tokens, private keys, payment details and personal data must be excluded or safely masked.

Avoid embedding large request bodies or entire domain objects in log events. Record the minimum information required to identify and investigate an event.

Structured logs are especially valuable in distributed systems because a centralized platform can filter events by service, environment, severity and request identifiers without parsing inconsistent message text.

sections.title: Correlation IDs, MDC and Distributed Request Tracking
Logging Configuration, Output Patterns and Runtime Log Control
sections.content:
# Logging Configuration, Output Patterns and Runtime Log Control

Spring Boot supports logging configuration through application properties and YAML. These settings allow teams to control log levels, output destinations and log message formatting without changing application source code.

Example:

```yaml
logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.example: DEBUG
  file:
    name: logs/inventory-service.log
  pattern:
    console: "%d{yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss} %-5level %logger - %msg%n"
```

The exact supported properties depend on the Spring Boot version and logging implementation. Review the version-specific logging documentation when configuring advanced behavior.

Logback-specific configuration can define appenders, encoders, rolling policies and package-level logger rules. A `logback-spring.xml` file is useful when configuration needs Spring Boot-specific extensions.

Spring Boot Actuator's loggers endpoint can inspect or change logger levels at runtime when the endpoint is enabled, exposed and properly secured.

Runtime level changes can be useful during incident investigation, but they should be temporary and controlled. Increasing DEBUG logging for a busy production service can produce large volumes of data and affect disk, network and storage consumption.

Define a controlled process for changing levels, recording who performed the change and restoring the intended configuration afterward.

Do not assume that changing a property file automatically reloads every logger setting. Verify the actual behavior of the selected logging implementation and configuration mechanism.

sections.title: Log Rotation, Retention Policies and Storage Management
sections.content:
# Log Rotation, Retention Policies and Storage Management

A production application can generate large amounts of log data. If logs are written continuously to a single file without rotation or cleanup, the file can consume all available disk space and cause application failures.

Log rotation divides output into manageable files based on size, time or a combination of both. Logback supports rolling appenders that can create new files according to a rolling policy.

A conceptual Logback configuration may use a rolling file appender with a time-based or size-based policy. The exact XML elements and properties must match the Logback version and selected appender.

A retention policy determines how long rotated logs remain available. For example, a service may retain a limited number of daily files locally while forwarding logs to centralized storage for longer retention.

In container environments, applications often write logs to standard output and standard error. The container runtime or orchestration platform can collect and rotate those streams. This avoids relying on a container's writable filesystem for long-term log retention.

Do not configure multiple independent rotation mechanisms without understanding their interaction. Application-level rotation and container-runtime rotation can conflict or create unexpected storage behavior.

Monitor disk usage, log volume and dropped log events. Define retention according to operational needs, legal requirements and organizational data policies.

A production logging design must balance investigation requirements with storage cost, performance and data protection.

Spring Boot Actuator Architecture and Operational Endpoints
sections.content:
# Spring Boot Actuator Architecture and Operational Endpoints

Spring Boot Actuator adds production-oriented management capabilities to an application. It exposes operational information through endpoints that can report health, metrics, application information, environment details and other diagnostics.

Actuator is commonly included through the `spring-boot-starter-actuator` dependency:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

A typical configuration exposes the health and info endpoints over HTTP:

```yaml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info
```

An endpoint is not necessarily available merely because the dependency exists. Endpoint availability, exposure, security configuration and application management settings all influence whether it can be accessed.

Common endpoints include `/actuator/health`, `/actuator/info`, `/actuator/metrics`, `/actuator/loggers` and `/actuator/prometheus` when the relevant integration is installed.

Actuator endpoints provide operational information; they do not automatically secure the application. Configure authentication, authorization, network restrictions and exposure policies before making management endpoints reachable.

Management endpoints may use the application's main HTTP server or a separate management port, depending on configuration. A separate port can provide an additional network boundary, but it still requires access control.

Use Actuator to support health monitoring and incident diagnosis. Expose only the endpoints that an operational requirement actually needs.

sections.title: Health Indicators, Readiness Probes and Liveness Probes
sections.content:
# Health Indicators, Readiness Probes and Liveness Probes

The Actuator health endpoint reports application health through health contributors and indicators. These can represent database connectivity, disk space, messaging systems and custom application dependencies.

A basic health request can be checked with:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/actuator/health
```

The response may include an overall status such as UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE or UNKNOWN. The exact components shown depend on configured indicators and health detail visibility.

Liveness and readiness answer different operational questions. Liveness indicates whether the application process should be restarted. Readiness indicates whether the application is prepared to receive traffic.

A service may be alive but not ready because it is still initializing or cannot access a required dependency. Restarting it repeatedly because of a readiness failure can make an incident worse.

Spring Boot supports dedicated health groups for liveness and readiness in supported configurations. These can be used by Kubernetes probes.

Example:

```yaml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
```

Configure Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes according to the actual application startup and recovery behavior.

Do not automatically include every external dependency in liveness. A temporary database outage should not necessarily cause Kubernetes to restart every application instance.

Use readiness to prevent traffic from reaching an instance that cannot serve requests, and design liveness to detect a genuinely stuck or unhealthy application process.

Prometheus Metrics Export and Monitoring Integration
sections.content:
# Prometheus Metrics Export and Monitoring Integration

Prometheus is a monitoring system that collects time-series metrics from configured targets. Spring Boot applications can expose Micrometer metrics in Prometheus format by including the appropriate registry integration.

For a Maven application, add the Prometheus registry dependency compatible with the application's Spring Boot and Micrometer versions:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

Expose the endpoint through Actuator:

```yaml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
```

The metrics endpoint can then be scraped by Prometheus when the application is reachable and the endpoint is properly configured:

```text
http://inventory-service:8080/actuator/prometheus
```

A Prometheus scrape configuration can identify the target:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: inventory-service
    metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - inventory-service:8080
```

The target address must be resolvable and reachable from the Prometheus deployment. In Kubernetes, service discovery or platform-specific scrape configuration may be more appropriate than static targets.

Verify that the endpoint returns Prometheus-formatted metrics and that Prometheus reports the target as healthy.

Protect the endpoint from public access. Monitoring systems should have only the network and permissions required to collect metrics.

Define useful alerts based on service-level objectives, such as request error rate, latency and resource saturation, rather than alerting on every available metric.

sections.title: Production Observability, Actuator Security and Hands-on Operations Lab
sections.content:
# Production Observability, Actuator Security and Hands-on Operations Lab

A production observability design combines logs, metrics and health information to help teams detect failures and understand application behavior.

First, add Spring Boot Actuator and configure only the required management endpoints. Expose health and information endpoints according to operational requirements, and add Prometheus integration when metrics scraping is needed.

A basic configuration might look like:

```yaml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: never
      probes:
        enabled: true
```

The configuration is only a starting point. Production security must also restrict network access and enforce authentication and authorization where appropriate.

Next, configure application logging. Use meaningful log levels, stable event names and correlation identifiers. Forward container output to an approved centralized logging platform and define retention limits.

Add a custom health indicator for a critical dependency. Test its successful response, timeout behavior and failure response. Verify that readiness reflects the application's ability to serve traffic without turning every dependency outage into a liveness failure.

Add Micrometer measurements for an important business operation. Confirm that the metric appears in the Actuator metrics endpoint and, when configured, in the Prometheus export.

Simulate an incident such as an unavailable external provider. Use health status to identify readiness problems, metrics to observe error rates and logs to inspect the failed operation and its correlation identifier.

Review security before deployment. Do not expose environment, configuration, heap dump or thread dump endpoints publicly. Restrict sensitive diagnostics to authorized operators because they may reveal internal configuration or application data.

The lab is complete when logs are searchable, metrics are collected, health checks reflect the correct operational state, sensitive endpoints are protected and an engineer can investigate a simulated failure without exposing confidential information.

sections.title: Production Lab Architecture, Business Requirements and System Boundaries
sections.content:
# Production Lab Architecture, Business Requirements and System Boundaries

This lab builds a production-oriented Inventory Management REST service using Java and Spring Boot. The objective is to connect the concepts learned throughout this stage into one coherent application rather than treating Java, Maven, dependency injection, REST, configuration and operations as isolated topics.

The application exposes APIs for creating inventory records, retrieving an item and updating available quantities. It uses a layered architecture so that HTTP handling, business rules and persistence responsibilities remain separate.

The main components are:

- Controller: accepts HTTP requests, validates request data and returns HTTP responses.
- Service: implements inventory business rules and coordinates operations.
- Repository: handles persistence and data access.
- DTO: defines the external API request and response contracts.
- Configuration: supplies environment-specific settings and infrastructure integration.
- Operational layer: provides logs, health information and metrics.

A request follows a controlled path:

```text
HTTP Client
    |
    v
REST Controller
    |
    v
Request Validation
    |
    v
Service Layer
    |
    v
Repository
    |
    v
Database
```

The production design must also consider authentication, authorization, transaction boundaries, failure handling, observability, configuration security and deployment repeatability.

Start by writing down the business requirements and API behavior. Define what constitutes a valid inventory item, which operations are permitted and how the application should respond when an item does not exist.

The lab is successful only when the application behaves correctly, can be tested independently, starts with controlled configuration and provides enough operational information for production support.

sections.title: Maven Project Bootstrap, Dependencies and Reproducible Builds
sections.content:
# Maven Project Bootstrap, Dependencies and Reproducible Builds

Create a Maven-based Spring Boot project with a clear package structure. Use a Spring Boot version compatible with the selected Java version and manage dependency versions through the Spring Boot parent or its dependency management.

A typical project layout is:

```text
inventory-service/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/example/inventory/
│   │   └── resources/
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/example/inventory/
└── Dockerfile
```

The application requires dependencies for web APIs, validation, persistence, Actuator and testing. Add the database driver and migration tooling appropriate to the selected database.

Example Maven dependency declarations:

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Use the Spring Boot Maven plugin to package an executable application artifact. Keep dependency versions consistent and avoid adding arbitrary versions to dependencies already managed by Spring Boot.

Build and test the project:

```bash
mvn clean verify
```

The `clean` phase removes previous build output, while `verify` runs the lifecycle through verification and executes configured checks.

For reproducible builds, control the Java toolchain, Maven version, dependency sources and build configuration. Commit the Maven wrapper so developers and CI can use a consistent Maven distribution.

Record the generated artifact version and checksum. A production deployment should use a known, tested artifact rather than an unverified local build.

sections.title: Domain Model Design, JPA Mapping and Database Constraints
Repository Implementation, Query Design and Persistence Boundaries
sections.content:
# Repository Implementation, Query Design and Persistence Boundaries

The repository layer provides the persistence boundary between application services and the database. Spring Data JPA can generate common database operations from repository interfaces.

Example:

```java
public interface InventoryRepository
        extends JpaRepository<InventoryItem, Long> {

    Optional<InventoryItem> findBySku(String sku);

    boolean existsBySku(String sku);
}
```

The repository provides standard operations such as saving, finding, deleting and paging records. Query methods can be derived from method names or implemented using explicit JPQL, native SQL or specifications where appropriate.

The service layer should depend on the repository interface rather than constructing database connections directly. This supports testing and keeps persistence details out of HTTP controllers.

Avoid returning JPA entities directly from API controllers. Entity structure is an internal persistence concern, while API response contracts should be deliberately designed and versioned.

For list operations, use pagination and sorting rather than retrieving an unlimited number of records. A large unbounded query can cause high memory usage and slow response times.

Consider transaction boundaries when multiple database operations must succeed or fail together. Use `@Transactional` at an appropriate service boundary and understand rollback behavior for checked and unchecked exceptions.

Watch for N+1 query problems when accessing related entities. Use appropriate fetch plans, projections or query strategies rather than blindly loading every relationship.

Verify repository behavior with database integration tests, including unique constraint violations, missing records and concurrent updates where relevant.

Database Configuration, Schema Migration and Connection Pooling
sections.content:
# Database Configuration, Schema Migration and Connection Pooling

The application should obtain its database connection details from external runtime configuration. Do not hardcode production credentials or database endpoints in Java source code.

Example configuration:

```yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: ${DB_URL}
    username: ${DB_USERNAME}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 15
      connection-timeout: 30000
```

The exact pool settings must be chosen according to database capacity, application concurrency and deployment size. A connection pool that is too large can overload the database when many application instances run simultaneously.

Use a migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase to manage schema changes. Store migration scripts in version control and apply them in a controlled deployment process.

Example migration filename:

```text
V1__create_inventory_items.sql
```

A migration might create the inventory table and its constraints. Later changes should be added as new migrations rather than silently changing previously applied scripts.

For production, review migration locking, rollback strategy, backward compatibility and the impact of schema changes on running application versions.

A safe rollout often uses an expand-and-contract approach: add compatible schema structures first, deploy code that can work with both old and new structures, then remove obsolete structures in a later release.

Verify database connectivity, migration completion, pool usage and query performance during deployment. A successful application startup alone does not prove that database capacity is sufficient under production traffic.

sections.title: Environment Configuration, Profiles and Secret Injection
sections.content:
# Environment Configuration, Profiles and Secret Injection

The same application artifact should be promoted through development, testing, staging and production. Environment-specific values should be supplied at runtime rather than creating separate application builds for each environment.

Use shared configuration for common settings and profile-specific configuration for legitimate differences. For example, development may use a local database while production uses a managed database endpoint.

Activate the intended profile through a deployment setting:

```text
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

Provide required values using environment variables or an approved external configuration mechanism:

```text
DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db.internal:5432/inventory
DB_USERNAME=inventory_app
DB_PASSWORD=<injected-secret>
```

The password placeholder represents a value supplied securely at runtime. Never commit real credentials to source control, Dockerfiles or ordinary application configuration.

For Kubernetes, use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration and Secrets or an integrated secret-management solution for sensitive values. Restrict access through RBAC and apply appropriate encryption and rotation controls.

Use `@ConfigurationProperties` to bind related application settings into typed configuration objects. Validate required properties during startup so that missing or invalid configuration fails early.

Document which settings are required, which have safe defaults and which are secret. Avoid maintaining different undocumented configuration names across environments.

After deployment, verify the selected profile and required configuration without printing secret values. Record the configuration revision associated with each deployment for reliable incident investigation.

sections.title: Automated Testing Strategy and Continuous Integration Quality Gates
Logging, Health Checks, Metrics and Production Observability
sections.content:
# Logging, Health Checks, Metrics and Production Observability

The inventory service needs operational visibility after deployment. Logs, health checks and metrics provide complementary information that helps engineers detect and investigate failures.

Use SLF4J for application logging and configure appropriate levels. Record meaningful events such as inventory creation, rejected requests and failed database operations. Include request or trace identifiers where possible.

Do not log credentials, access tokens or complete sensitive request payloads. Keep log messages useful, structured and consistent.

Add Spring Boot Actuator and expose only the required management endpoints. Health checks should indicate whether the application is alive and whether it is ready to serve traffic.

Configure liveness and readiness separately. A temporary external dependency failure should not automatically cause every application instance to restart.

Use Micrometer to measure request counts, latency, failures and important business operations. Export metrics to Prometheus when the monitoring architecture requires it.

Define alerts around service behavior, such as elevated error rates, excessive request latency, resource saturation and sustained readiness failures.

Monitor database connection pool usage and dependency latency as well as JVM memory and garbage collection behavior.

Protect operational endpoints with network restrictions and appropriate access controls. Avoid exposing environment details, heap dumps, thread dumps or sensitive configuration publicly.

A useful production dashboard should help answer whether the service is available, whether requests are succeeding, whether performance is degrading and which dependency may be responsible.

sections.title: Container Image Creation, Runtime Configuration and Docker Validation
sections.content:
# Container Image Creation, Runtime Configuration and Docker Validation

Package the tested Spring Boot application as a container image. The image should contain the application artifact and the runtime components required to execute it, while environment-specific settings remain external.

A simple multi-stage Dockerfile can build and run the application:

```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B clean package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/*.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]
```

This is an illustrative build pattern. In a production pipeline, run tests and quality checks before creating the runtime image, and use a controlled, supported base image.

Avoid embedding passwords, environment-specific endpoints or private keys into image layers. Supply runtime configuration when the container starts.

Build the image:

```bash
docker build -t inventory-service:1.0 .
```

Run it with a selected profile:

```bash
docker run --rm \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev \
  inventory-service:1.0
```

Validate the container startup logs, application port, health endpoint and database connectivity. Check that the container process runs as a non-root user where practical and that filesystem permissions are appropriate.

Use image scanning and controlled image registries. Pin base-image versions and record the resulting image digest so that deployments can identify the exact image that was tested.

A container being in a running state does not prove the application is ready. Use an appropriate health check and verify application-level readiness.

sections.title: CI/CD Deployment Promotion, Kubernetes Readiness and Rollback
sections.content:
# CI/CD Deployment Promotion, Kubernetes Readiness and Rollback

A production delivery pipeline should build, test, package, scan and publish the application before deploying it. The same tested artifact should be promoted through environments rather than rebuilt with different source or dependencies for production.

A typical delivery flow is:

```text
Source Commit
    |
    v
Compile and Unit Tests
    |
    v
Integration Tests
    |
    v
Quality and Security Checks
    |
    v
Build Container Image
    |
    v
Publish Image
    |
    v
Deploy to Environment
    |
    v
Health Verification
    |
    v
Release Approval
```

In Kubernetes, a Deployment defines the desired application replicas and the container image. ConfigMaps and Secrets provide runtime configuration, while Services provide stable network access to pods.

Configure readiness probes so traffic is sent only to pods that can serve requests. Configure liveness probes to detect an application that is genuinely unable to recover.

Use rolling updates with suitable availability settings. Confirm that the new version becomes ready before the old version is removed.

A rollback should restore a known-good application version and compatible configuration. Database migrations require special planning because a code rollback cannot always reverse a schema change safely.

Record the deployed image digest, source revision, configuration revision and rollout result.

After deployment, run smoke tests against important API operations and verify logs, metrics and health status. Do not mark a release successful merely because the Kubernetes Deployment command completed.

sections.title: Production Incident Simulation, Acceptance Criteria and Final Release Review
sections.content:
# Production Incident Simulation, Acceptance Criteria and Final Release Review

The final exercise validates the inventory application under realistic operational failure conditions. The goal is to prove that the application can be diagnosed and recovered, not simply that it starts successfully.

Simulate a database connectivity failure by using an invalid database endpoint in a controlled test environment. Observe startup behavior, health indicators and application logs. Confirm that the failure is reported clearly and that secrets are not exposed.

Restore the correct database configuration and restart or redeploy the service. Verify that the application becomes ready and that database operations succeed.

Simulate an invalid API request. Confirm that validation rejects the request with a suitable HTTP status and a consistent error response. Verify that unexpected server exceptions are logged internally without exposing stack traces to clients.

Test a missing inventory record and a duplicate SKU. Confirm that the API returns the expected not-found and conflict responses.

Review application metrics and identify request count, latency, failure rate and JVM measurements. Verify that Prometheus can collect the expected metrics when configured.

Review the deployment record and confirm that the running image corresponds to the approved build. Check the selected profile, configuration revision, health probes and rollback procedure.

Final acceptance criteria:

- The application compiles and passes automated verification.
- REST endpoints follow the documented HTTP contract.
- Business rules and database constraints protect inventory data.
- Configuration is externalized and secrets are not committed.
- Logs and operational metrics provide useful diagnostic evidence.
- Health checks represent readiness and liveness correctly.
- The container image is reproducible and securely configured.
- The deployment pipeline records artifact and release information.
- A failed deployment can be detected and safely rolled back.

Complete a final release review with the development, testing and operations teams. Document known limitations, operational ownership and recovery instructions.

The lab is complete when the application is tested, deployable, observable and supportable—not merely when the JAR or container image has been generated.
